subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, March 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. Dunning for committee of supply.
Mr.J.T.THORSON (Selkirk): Mr.Speaker, the central theme of this debate on foreign policy has been the relationship that should exist between Canada and Great Britain in time of war. This question is of supreme importance to the Canadian people; there can be no issue of as great importance to them as that of peace or war.
Last Friday I moved the second reading of the bill which stands in my name on the order paper. The principle of that bill is that Great Britain cannot automatically commit Canada to war, that Canada can be committed to war only by a declaration of war made by his majesty with specific reference to Canada and only upon the advice of his majesty's government in Canada. This is the first time that this issue has been placed in a concrete form before the Canadian parliament. It has never yet been squarely faced by the Canadian people.
I made it perfectly clear that I was not advocating a policy of neutrality under all circumstances. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) very clearly pointed out in the magnificent address which he made on Friday:
There is all the difference in the world between the right to neutrality and the exercise of that right-between the right to neutrality and a policy of neutrality.
While I am not advocating a policy of neutrality, I do very strongly assert, in the name of the Canadian people, Canada's right to neutrality. How Canada will exercise that right once it has been acquired is a question for Canada to decide under the circumstances of each case. In my opinion Canadians must face the reality that they must decide the issue of peace or war themselves and not leave that decision to be made for them by another country. It is not enough that we should merely decide the extent of our participation in war. That does not give us the freedom of choice which belongs to us as a matter of
Foreign Policy-Mr. Thorson

right. The decision of this issue is a matter of national responsibility that we as a Canadian nation must eventually face.
The Prime Minister indicated very clearly that he understood the reasons behind the proposal which has been made, when he said, as reported on page 2425 of Hansard:
I recognize that those who are advocating and supporting the proposal to which I have referred regard it as a logical consequence, a necessary implication, of our long evolution toward self-government. It registers the conclusion that it would not be consistent with the present relationship of the members of the commonwealth to hold that the king would act for Canada as regards war and peace on the advice of any other one of his governments, but not on the advice of his government in Canada itself. It is put forward as a recognition of the necessity of the people, the parliament, the government of this country accepting adult responsibility for a course that so vitally affects them, rather than throwing that responsibility on other members of the commonwealth or their governments.
The Prime Minister gave strong support to the fundamental purpose of the bill when he made it clear that Canada could not accept a policy of automatic commitment to war or automatic participation in war regardless of the issues involved, and I am quite certain that Canadians throughout Canada will welcome that statement. They will also welcome the statement made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) -that Canada must not adopt a position of inferiority or be used as a pawn on the international chessboard. On behalf of thousands of Canadians who think as I do in these matters, I gratefully acknowledge these statements of principle and thank both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition for them. I should like also to thank the Minister of Justice for the statement he made on Friday as reported on page 2467 of Hansard. He said:
I have sympathy, I must admit, with the bill of my good friend the lion, member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) that if Canada takes part in a war the government of Canada should itself declare accordingly. Anyway, it will be for parliament to decide what part Canada should have in the war.
Then the Minister of Justice went on to say:
The present situation, I confess, is perhaps not satisfactory. It is one of the problems that remain to be solved and it will be solved as all the other problems of the commonwealth have been solved.
With that statement I entirely agree. I agree that the present situation is not satisfactory, but I also believe with him that this question will be solved as we have solved so many other questions affecting our national status.

The Prime Minister said that he did not himself think that at the present time it was either necessary or desirable to seek enactment of this legislation, and he gave a number of reasons for this opinion. Naturally I have the highest regard for this expression of view. Indeed, there are differences of opinion as to the necessity for any such legislation. There is a large body of constitutional opinion in this country which thinks that no legislation is necessary. Personally I share this point of view. I have stated it on a number of occasions. Indeed, I think I am the first person in this House of Commons to have declared that Canada is not automatically at war when Great Britain is at war. In my opinion, since the Balfour declaration of 1926, his majesty can act for Canada in the matter of a declaration of war only upon the advice of his majesty's ministers in Canada. This right is inherent in the concept of the British commonwealth of nations. If the British nations are autonomous nations, if they are all equal in status to one another, and are in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their affairs, it must follow that no British nation can commit another British nation automatically to war. This state of affairs may create anomalies. It may seem to be a peculiar relationship. But the relationship that exists between the British nations in that entity known as the British commonwealth of nations is a peculiar one. There is no term known to the law that adequately and properly describes that relationship. I think it can be said that while we owe allegiance to one king and that the person of the king is indivisible, the crown is divisible; for his majesty wears his crown in several rights. He is king of Canada as well as king of Great Britain, and in matters affecting Canada he acts upon the advice of his Canadian ministers. That is consistent with the general British constitutional position that when his majesty performs an executive act of government he performs that executive act only upon the advice of his responsible ministers; in his capacity as king of Canada he cannot make a declaration that affects Canada except upon the advice of his Canadian ministers. This, in my opinion, is sound constitutional doctrine. It is inherent in our status as a self-governing nation; it is inherent in our status as a member of the British commonwealth of nations. I agree that there are differences of opinion in this regard; but in the view that I have just expressed I am supported by a well-known authority on constitutional law.

Foreign Policy

Mr. Thorson
Doctor Ollivier, law clerk of the House of Commons, in his book Canada a Sovereign Country, says:
The question has often been asked: "When England is at war, is Canada at war?" We have no hesitation in giving a negative answer. In writing about treaties we have demonstrated that Canada is bound only by those it has signed; we have shown also that the king's advisers in the United Kingdom cannot give him advice respecting dominion affairs; consequently the king can declare war in the name of Canada only if our Canadian ministers so advise him.	*
It may be that when I express this constitutional opinion the majority opinion is not the same as mine.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We hope not.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But I cannot see how it would be possible to express a different constitutional opinion that would be consistent with our relationship to one another in the British commonwealth of nations.
There are in Canada a number of constitutional lawyers who express a different opinion; in their view Canada has the capacity to acquire the right of neutrality; but they say that since Canada has not yet exercised her powers in that respect and taken the necessary steps to acquire the right of neutrality, Canada does not yet-possess that right. In their view Canada does not possess the right until she acquires it by asserting it by legislative action, defining the manner in which action shall or shall not foe taken in the name of Canada. It is their view that prior to the new status acquired by Canada a declaration of war made by his majesty upon the advice of his ministers at Westminster would be automatic and would bind all the dominions. This was the view in 1914 when a declaration of war made by Great Britain automatically bound the dominions. These authorities contend that as a matter of law this legal situation remains unchanged until legal steps are taken by Canada to change it. They take the view that under the statute of Westminster Canada has the power to declare that the old legal status no longer exists, if Canada wishes to exercise the right which she has under that statute. Their view is that the statute of Westminster gives power to Canada only in respect of action that this parliament might take in the future. According to them, it does not repeal any existing laws affecting Canada; these laws remain as they were until Canada, in the exercise of the new powers given to her by the statute of Westminster, makes the necessary changes. It is therefore the view of these authorities that as a matter of law, under the powers of the statute of Westminster, Canada can make the declaration that is contained 71492-159
in the bill which I have proposed. They take the view that a declaration of war made by his majesty on the advice of his ministers at Westminster binds all the dominions except those which have asserted that they have the right to decide the manner in which a declaration of war shall be binding upon them. This bill was, therefore, introduced to make it perfectly plain and clear that as far as Canada is concerned Great Britain no longer has the power to commit Canada automatically to war.

speechtext:
Then I shall confine myself to the [principle involved and not make reference specifically to the bill.
It is I think highly desirable that if there are any doubts as to the right of Canada to assert her right to neutrality, these doubts should be removed by legislative action by this parliament. It is desirable that the right to neutrality should be declared and placed beyond dispute. If those of us who believe that we already have the right are correct in our assumption, then legislation of this sort would merely be a statutory declaration of an existing constitutional fact. If on the other hand those who take the contrary view are correct, then we are, indeed in an anomalous position. If they are right, I submit that as a matter of national safety parliament should declare, not that Canada should be neutral, but that Canada has the right to be neutral if Canada wishes to be so. Why should Canada be automatically thrown into a state of war by a government that is not her own? Why should we continue to delegate this supreme power over the lives of our Canadian people to the Prime Minister of Great Britain, no matter how we may admire him, no matter how great a person he may be? Yet that is what we are doing, if those who hold this view are right in their assumption.
In my opinion this is an issue that the Canadian people must face. We have not yet faced the problem squarely, but we must do so if we are to discharge our duty as members of the Canadian nation. I am convinced that this decision will have to be made as an inevitable step in our march towards

Foreign Policy-Mr. Thorson
full realization of our status and our responsibility as a self-governing nation. How can we as a Canadian nation insist upon full autonomy in all matters that affect us internally and refuse responsibility for the decision of the issue of peace or war, the greatest responsibility that we can owe to our people?
The assertion of the right to neutrality is in accord with the spirit of the British constitution; it is the right of all peoples who live under it to determine in every respect the policies that they will follow. It is also the duty of people who live under the British constitution to exercise their rights. There is no one in this house who more ardently admires the British constitution than I do. It is the greatest instrument of self-government that the world has ever known. It breathes liberty, but it is based upon responsibility. In all things the people themselves, through their elected representatives, decide on policy. It would be more consistent with the spirit of the British constitution to accept the proposal that has been advanced than to reject it.
Nor do I agree that the adoption of such a proposal would weaken our relationship with Great Britain. If we came into action side by side with Great Britain it would be as a result of free choice made by the people of Canada. It should not be otherwise. We are freely associated with the other British nations in that entity known as the British commonwealth of nations; all our actions in that association should be the result of free choice upon our part-and not otherwise.
Nor do I agree that it would be playing into the hands of the dictators, or weakening the position of Great Britain, to adopt this proposal. No one in this house has greater respect for Great Britain and what she stands for than I have. If Great Britain's existence were involved, Canada would not hesitate to come to her assistance. May I say I have not contented myself with giving lip service to the British constitution or to Great Britain; I served three years in the forces. For eighteen months of that period I served with the British forces in France, seconded to the British army from the Canadian army. It was stated the other day by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) that before my people came to Canada this country had been settled by British born people. May I tell the hon. member for Broadview that men of my racial origin in Canada enlisted in the Canadian forces to a greater extent in proportion to their numbers than did the native born people of Canada as a whole. They
I Mr. Thorson.]
have played their part in demanding the rights and liberties of this nation, but they have also been prepared to do their duty in defence of such rights. Let no man in this house challenge my right to speak as a Canadian, with the voice of Canada.
I do not for one moment fear the consequences of acquiring for Canada the right of neutrality. Whether Canada will exercise that right or not will depend upon the issues involved. I am not afraid of the course that Canada will follow. I am content that this issue be left to Canada; it belongs to' Canada. We must face the consequences of whatever decision we make. The right of decision in the matter of neutrality belongs to Canada, and the duty of exercising that right must remain with Canada.
This debate has served a most useful purpose; for it'will focus attention on the importance of our foreign policy to the life and welfare of the Canadian people. We in this house are the representatives of the Canadian people, and we are responsible to them for the decisions we make. In such issues as those of peace or war there are no differences between the Canadian people, no differences of language, creed or racial origin. They are all Canadians, and we are charged with the duty and responsibility of safeguarding their interests and their welfare.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, with a question: How can we discharge our supreme responsibility to our people, that of keeping them out of war, as long as we leave the decision of that great issue in the hands of a government that is not our own?

The province of Quebec has not that narrowminded attitude which is so frequently pictured elsewhere. In looking back over the political history of my province I remember an incident which occurred during a provincial election. At the time the city of Three Rivers was composed almost entirely of French Canadians. It had one Jewish family and one English speaking family. The representative elected to the legislature of that province was the single Jewish member of the community, a man by the name of Hart. I merely quote that instance to show that the province of Quebec is generous in its treatment of minorities in regard to political considerations.
I also want to make the suggestion that the people of Quebec are exceptionally attached to the monarchical form of government. They are particularly attached to the British crown, probably more so than any other section of this dominion. I think very few members of this house realize that the people living in the province of Quebec have known no other form of government than a constitutional monarchy during their whole history. They have never lived under any other form of government, and I know they would be the last people in Canada who would desire to depart from that form of government; therefore their attachment to British institutions and to the British crown.
It is not my intention to follow the remarks of the last speaker (Mr. Thorson). I quite disagree with his suggestions and his conclusions. speechtext:
His constitutional arguments leave me entirely unmoved, and I do not see that they will have any effect upon citizens of Canada who may read them, as to whether or not we should be in a position to declare our neutrality.
During the course of my remarks I hope to be able to show that we are a part of, and desire to remain a part of, the British commonwealth of nations. I recognize the fact that our imperial relationships are undergoing very important changes. We are living in a world of change, and our attitude must change from day to day.
I had intended to make reference to the observations of the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe). In fact I had intended to suggest, in his own language, words to this effect:
(Translation): It is with deep regret that I read the remarks of the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe). I had hoped that all hon. members, particularly those from my province, would have approved the statement of the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and recognized the need of full agreement on a subject of this nature. I cannot share the opinions enunciated by my hon. friend from Laval-Two Mountains and I do not think that they represent the point of view of the province of Quebec.
(Text) I say this in all sincerity. I do not think the remarks of the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains represent the genuine feeling of his people during the crises through which we have passed, and the one through which we are now passing. I suggest that in Canada we should strive to put our own house in order. We have many vital problems to be discussed and to be settled, and so far as possible we should endeavour to settle them, and along permanent lines. I could set forth many of them, but time will not permit. We desire the unity of the British commonwealth of nations. We feel that that unity is a vital factor in the shaping of world destinies. So also is unity within our own borders essential to the effective development not only of our own nation but also of the British commonwealth of nations. I hope the problems we have with us to-day will soon disappear, that in Canada we shall be able to present a united front as Canadians, and thus be a larger contributing force towards the solution of the problems of the commonwealth to which we belong.
It was my intention to delve back into history, and to trace our steps in nationhood to the point we have now reached. It was my intention to show how after 1870 British

foreign policy had been influenced to some extent by imperialism, and how that influence had continued almost down to the early years of the present century. An outstanding example of that imperialistic tendency is exemplified in the war in South Africa. If gold and diamonds had not been found within the reaches of South Africa, there would have been no South African war. The imperial tendency towards expansion into countries where trade would be profitable and beneficial caused England to reach out into many parts of the world where otherwise she would not have reached, if in those parts trade had not been to her benefit. That was the imperialistic tendency of the age, and we in Canada played our part in its development. We took our part in the fighting of the South African war, and indeed that was one of the first periods in our history when we made a direct contribution towards the battles of what was then the British empire.
After that the imperial attitude changed somewhat, and looking back on history we find growing up certain relationships between Canada and the mother country, relationships brought about to a great extent through imperial, or as they were first called, colonial conferences, the first of which took place in 1887, and the second-I had not known this fact until I made a study of the matter- in 1894 in the city of Ottawa. The holding of the conference here showed a growth in the minds of the British people and in the minds of peoples throughout the empire, as it was then known, of a realization of the importance of this dominion.
Later we notice that colonial conferences gave way to imperial conferences, and then imperial conferences gave way to something larger and more representative of the feeling of our commonwealth of nations. In 1917 there was a growth and development which, probably unnoticed at that time, but to-day has a considerable degree of significance. I refer to the imperial war cabinet, created in 1917, when all parts of the empire were represented in London for the purpose of more effectively carrying on and bringing to a conclusion the great war then in progress. On that occasion the British Prime Minister sat at the head of the table, not as one over and above those assembled, but as one whose presence was described by the Latin expression primus inter pares, first among equals, which shows the position which Canada occupied at that time.
Then there was the further development after the war when, in the signing of the treaty of Versailles, Canada was definitely placed in the category of an independent

Foreign Policy-Mr. Walsh
nation capable of making a separate contribution on her own behalf so far as the signing of treaties with other nations is concerned. I believe it was during the discussion of the treaty of Versailles that Sir Robert Borden, the then Prime Minister of Canada, was first to use the expression " imperial commonwealth." And now we have this great empire recognized as the commonwealth of British nations. It will be noticed from all I have said that the actual settlement of the question as to the body responsible for foreign affairs and foreign policy of the empire or the commonwealth has not as yet been settled. It is something which must ibe settled. It is the lack of settlement in that regard which is causing some concern, and which gives rise to a debate of the kind in which we are at present engaged.
In 1931, when the statute of Westminster was signed, we reached the pinnacle towards which we were climbing, that of almost complete nationhood. We claimed new rights as we advanced step by step to nationhood. I ask hon. members this question: Did not those new rights carry with them new obligations and new responsibilities? With the enactment of the statute of Westminster in 1931, Canada was recognized as having attained the full status of nationhood, as being a nation within a nation.
As I have said, those new rights and privileges carried with them new obligations. Canada's attitude towards other nations, in fact her new attitude towards most questions, both internal and external, had to be defined or redefined. To discuss these questions we must of necessity contemplate questions of armament, defence at home, defence abroad, defence on land and sea, our political position in the British commonwealth, our geographical position, our internal economy. Within recent months there has been a noticeable activity in the Department of National Defence-I make no reference here, of course, to the Bren gun or any episode of that nature. Not only will this involve expense, but it will raise again the issue of our national unity. The question that might then be discussed is this: Are we a nation? Are we accepted by other countries as a nation? Or do we still fall short of the complete definition of that term? I think the answer at the present time is that we are not a nation in the usual acceptance of the term; and that, I think, is the general opinion which has been expressed so far during the course of this debate.
I had intended to take up the question of foreign policy with particular reference to the resignation of Anthony Eden, an event which
involved Canada as much as it did any other part of the commonwealth. He resigned; a new foreign office minister was appointed, and no doubt Canada was not consulted. This event reflected a change not only in the cabinet in England but also in the attitude as to Great Britain's foreign policy; and, if we are to accept the principles laid down by most speakers in this debate, with which I find myself in agreement, Canada was somewhat involved in that change of attitude.
So far as a foreign policy for Canada is concerned, there are three possible alternatives. One is that of isolation. I recall that in the speech from the throne in January, 1937, the government put these words into the mouth of his excellency:
The international situation continues to give much ground for anxiety.
I think the Prime Minister will agree with me that those words are just as true to-day as when they were uttered in January, 1937. The present government recognizes the situation; we in this parliament recognize it, and we discuss what our reaction will be in certain eventualities. The first alternative of isolation I think I can immediately dismiss. I do not think any member of this house, indeed anyone in Canada, would suggest that isolation was a safe and sound policy to pursue or even to contemplate at the present time. Canada is not in a position to isolate herself from the rest of the world or from the British commonwealth of nations. Canada must, in her own interests, maintain her position within the commonwealth. Therefore I dismiss the suggestion of isolation.
I come next to the position that we might take shelter under the Monroe doctrine. The Monroe doctrine is a much misunderstood document. It was merely a statement made to congress away back in 1823 by the then president, James Monroe. It read, in part'
[DOT]-that the American continents are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers.
And further:
With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power, we have not interfered nor shall not interfere.
That was the policy declared by the then president of the United States. It is a policy which has been reiterated by almost every president of the United States since, and I have no doubt it is the policy on which they propose to act even to-day. But it is merely a statement of policy, and it is unilateral, not a multilateral policy in any sense of the term. We therefore should not seek too much refuge under what is generally termed the Monroe doctrine.
Foreign Policy-Mr. Walsh

The President of the United States, speaking in Canada in the latter part of last summer, made certain statements respecting Canada. He said:
The Dominion of Canada is part of the sisterhood of the British empire. X give to you assurance that the people of the United States will not stand idly by if domination of Canadian soil is threatened by any other empire.
I want hon. members to notice, first, that the United States, our closest and best neighbour, readily acknowledges Canada, not as a nation, but as part of the sisterhood of the British empire'. In the second place I want to make this suggestion, that President Roosevelt's words on that occasion cannot be construed as guaranteeing full and absolute support to Canada if Canada should be found at war. United States support is to be given to Canada, only if Canada is invaded by some foreign power, and their intervention then we recognize would be just as much in their own interests as in ours. The United States could not afford to have three thousand miles of frontier controlled or possessed by any other nation than Canada herself, in conformity with her present position of a member state of the British commonwealth of nations.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"If domination of Canadian soil is threatened by any other empire." "Threatened" presumably meant threatened by invasion. We all understand the meaning of the word "threatened." If Canada were threatened, the United States would feel it her duty to protect her own frontiers by not allowing any other empire to establish itself north of the present boundary between Canada and the United States.
I would go further and suggest that we have no guarantees under the Monroe doctrine. Naturally we feel a certain confidence in having such a good neighbour to the south of us, and naturally we have a certain confidence in the statements that have been made from time to time by the President of the United States. But I do not feel that Canada as a whole desires to take refuge under the protection of the Monroe doctrine. In the first place it is not as absolutely safe as we would desire it; and then it might lead to repercussions which no red-blooded Canadian would like to contemplate.
The third alternative is to retain our place within the British commonwealth of nations. This seems to be Canada's real place-her culture, her trade, and a common policy of

promoting peace and security for a troubled world. Providing a separate defence for Canada is in my estimation beside the question. We cannot do that. But we can provide a defence for Canada in conformity with the defence of the empire or the commonwealth as a whole.
We often hear whispers, Mr. Speaker, that the British nation is in a decadent state, that this great commonwealth is about to collapse and fall to pieces. With these statements I am in utter disagreement. History has shown that similar statements were made many years ago; yet the British empire is still a great and potent force throughout the world. I took a clipping from one of the English papers a week or two ago containing statements made in those earlier days which would almost lead to the belief that the collapse of the then empire was imminent. William Pitt in his day said:
There is scarcely anything around us but ruin and despair.
Wilberforce, in the early 1800's, said:
I dare not marry, the future is so dark and unsettled.
Lord Grey in 1819 said he "believed everything was tending to a convulsion;" and the Duke of Wellington on his deathbed "thanked God he would be spared from seeing the consummation of ruin that is gathering around." Disraeli, that great figure of the mid-nineteenth century, said on one occasion:
In industry, commerce and agriculture there is no hope.
Lord Shaftesbury capped the climax by saying, in 1848:
Nothing can save the British empire from shipwreck.
Yet here we are to-day, enjoying apparently a healthy prosperity in a new age as a commonwealth of nations, the successor to the British empire; and I feel that those who at this time cry despair have little confidence in themselves and less confidence in those who are to succeed them. Listening some time ago in the city of Toronto to an address, I heard quoted two lines of which I am reminded every time I hear the national anthem, and on occasions when despair is evident in the faces and the sentiments of certain of our fellow citizens:
Breed ye the sons your fathers bred And God will save the king.
I would go further, and say that He will save not only the king but Canada and the commonwealth to which we belong.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
It was the Prime Minister, if I remember correctly, who on May 24 last year, at page 3182 of Hansard, made a statement in the house as follows:
No course of action adopted by the United Kingdom in foreign affairs can fail to have repercussions, great or small, upon Canada and the other members of the commonwealth of nations. The problem of adjustment this fact presents is one of the most difficult and complicated that faces Canada and the other parts of the commonwealth as well.
The statement, which I consider accurate, is one which sends out somewhat of a challenge. I am still firmly convinced that the hope of Canada is within this commonwealth of nations. There we can get that peace and security which we crave for our country and which we desire for our children and those who are to follow them. I believe that the greatest and most potent force in the world for peace to-day is a strengthened and revitalized British commonwealth of nations, of which Canada should be an important if not a dominant factor.
During the course of this debate many statements have been made setting forth Canada's peculiar position. It has made me happy to observe the optimism which prevails and the manner in which this question has been presented to the country. I feel sure that as a result of this debate the people will have more confidence both in their leaders in this house and in the future of our nation. What has been said by way of defining Canada's position will not make war more imminent; if anything it will have a retarding effect as far as war is concerned. It will show to the world what Canada conceives her position to be; it will show to the world that she intends to remain an important factor in the commonwealth of British nations. The rest of the world will know that Britain, standing for peace, is probably in a position to assure it.
I place before you these three possibilities. As regards the first two, we are not in possession of all the facts which have been communicated to our government; therefore some of my remarks may be a little beside the point. Our conjectures may cause us to lean to the third alternative which I am presenting, even if we cannot arrive at a definite conclusion. We can and must strive for peace. With the British empire and the United States coming more closely together and speaking with an almost common voice in relation to foreign affairs, (there is good hope for peace within the English speaking world, and possibly
in the world at large. In this effort Canada has a definite part to play, because of her geographical position north of the United States of America and midway between Europe and Asia. We can reaffirm our support of the League of Nations, effectively strengthened and prepared to secure peace through conciliatory and not coercive methods. We can reassert our belief in the supremacy of the Canadian parliament to decide, in its own way and in the light of the facts available at the time, to what extent Canada shall be involved in another war. These can be guiding principles in the realm of foreign policy.
Canada is still a British country, a member state of the British commonwealth of nations. Canada intends to remain in the empire and will not endeavour to escape its responsibilities as a British nation. Of course there are differences of opinion as to the scope of our responsibilities, but none as to their character. Therefore I have had occasion to hope, as I have listened to this debate, that little or no differences of opinion exist as to our responsibility or our immediate course. There may be some difference of opinion as to the character of our responsibilities, but this is a question which will be settled, when the time comes, by the parliament of Canada.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The present debate has revealed a remarkable unanimity in all parts of the house on certain broad principles of foreign policy. There are many things about which we disagree, but I am sure that the similarity of opinion on some of the fundamental issues has been a revelation to most of us.
May I enumerate three points of view which seem to have met with general acceptance by all groups in this house.
First, Canadians should have the right to decide the part that Canada will take in the event of Great Britain becoming involved in a war. There have been some differences of opinion, of course, as to whether we have the right to remain neutral, and as to whether we can remain neutral without seceding from the British commonwealth of nations, but the general principle that the Canadian people- and they alone-should determine the part they will play in any war in which Great Britain becomes involved seems to have met with general agreement.
Second, it seems to be the consensus that Canada's main contribution in the event of war will be economic, and that her military contribution will at best be relatively small.
2518	COMMONS
Foreign Policy-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
Third, opposition to conscription has been expressed by the leaders of all the groups in this house, it being pointed out that conscription was of little or no value during the last war and it aroused antagonism and friction out of all proportion to any value that it might have had.
Since there seems to be general agreement on the three points upon which I have briefly touched, I shall take them for granted and proceed to develop the line of reasoning pursued by my deskmate. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) pointed out that collective security had failed, largely due to the fact that the vested interests in the great powers fear people's political movements much more than they fear fascism. He pointed out that some nations which were now most afraid of Hitler had helped to build him up to his present strength in the hope that he would be a bulwark against radical tendencies in Europe. Now, like Frankenstein, these same powers find themselves in danger of being destroyed by the very monster which they created. My colleague concluded by making a plea for a return to collective security as the only hope of establishing world peace and world order. It seems to me that a return to collective peace action-not collective war action-will involve the acceptance of two major principles. The first is that nations desirous of peace shall express their willingness to rectify the mistakes of the treaty of Versailles and shall immediately take cognizance of those economic causes which have driven certain nations of Europe to resort to dictatorships. In my opinion, it is no accident that the "have-not" nations, Italy, Germany and Japan, are also the fascist nations. A former German Chancellor, Doctor Stresemann, said of his country, "Germany must expand or explode." It was failure to make it possible that such expansion should go on peaceably and legitimately that brought about the recent acts of aggression and lawlessness. It is not enough to say, "Stop Hitler!" We must be prepared to deal with the causes that have produced Hitler.
The second principle in collective peace action is the willingness of the nations who desire peace to act collectively, not to maintain the status quo but to act collectively to make any resort to force an unprofitable venture. It will be argued that such collective action will involve sacrifices. I admit that, but I do submit that the sacrifices will be infinite-

simal compared to the sacrifices that would follow from another world war. Collective peace action may mean the making of economic concessions and colonial adjustments. It may mean our participation in economic sanctions against an aggressor nation. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group have never objected to this country being asked to make sacrifices of that kind. On February 19, 1937, speaking in the House of Commons against increased defence estimates I said:
I object to increased armaments. If they *were a contribution to some collective security system it would be an entirely different matter. What this house is being asked to do is to pay for the weak and vacillating attitude that has been taken by the government in connection with international affairs. I, for one, will never give either my voice or my vote to send young men out to lay down their lives because of the incompetency and, in many cases, the stupidity of those who have directed the foreign policy of this country.
It is because we have been convinced that the sacrifices the Canadian people have been called upon to make have been directed, not towards peace but towards war that we have consistently opposed them in this house.
Canada, in view of her vast economic resources, can play a decisive role in any collective peace action which the nations of the world are prepared to take. It was recognized as far back as 1920 that Canada's main contribution to collective security was her strategic economic position. It will be remembered that Canada made a reservation of article 16 of the covenant of the League of Nations, which expressly stated that, in the event of military measures being brought against an aggressor, the council of the league should take account of the geographical situation of each state. Canada has never been seriously thought of as a military power who might wield a great influence in European affairs, but we are a great source of those raw materials necessary for the waging of war, and as such, we can play an important role in world affairs. It was because of our failure to signify our willingness to play such a role in 1935 that we contributed to the conquest of Ethiopia and the ultimate destruction of the League of Nations. The present government must accept some responsibility for the fact that oil sanctions, the only effective sanctions that might have been applied, were not put into effect against Italy. During the past four years, despite all our protestations of peace, this country has continued to be a

Foreign Policy-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
source of supply for the aggressor nations who are rearming with a view to challenging the league and of all that the league has stood for.

Of the total of 1938 exports, seventy per cent was for aeroplanes which were sold by manufacturers in this country to the Turkish government. As it later developed, these aeroplanes did not really reach Turkey but instead landed in Spain.
Close perusal of these statistics will I think bring forth three questions. One is, why are we sending implements of war to countries outside the British commonwealth of nations? Is it that we have more than enough in Canada? Is it that they do not need them in Great Britain? A recent editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press made the statement-I cannot vouch for its authenticity-that last fall there were in Canada only six Hawker Hurricane bombing planes, and since then one has been destroyed on the Pacific, so that there are now only five. If this be true, how could we afford to send thirty-four military aeroplanes last year to the Turkish government? In my opinion no manufacturer of implements of war should be allowed to sell or export these instruments of death to any foreign power until the Canadian government and the British government are perfectly satisfied that their own needs and requirements have been supplied, and that the recipients of these munitions are friendly powers. In

this matter of exports of implements of war, the time has come when the Canadian government ought to take a very firm stand.
The second question arising out of these facts is that these exports of war material challenge the sincerity of the present government in asking for repeated increases in votes for national defence. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation each year have asked why the increased expenditure for national defence, and in reply we have had horrible pictures painted of bombing planes destroying Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. Either we are afraid of certain aggressive nations or we are not. If we are not afraid of them, then all talk of the need for increased defence expenditures is nonsense. If we are afraid of them, by what logic do we continue to supply those same nations with the materials with which they might destroy our cities and citizens?
A third question arising from a study of these figures is that some day-heaven grant it may never come-we may be asking Canadian citizens to engage in a war in which their bodies will be lacerated and torn by the very material which is now being sent out of Canada in order to increase the dividends of certain Canadian concerns and swell the profits of United States investors. Will it be a great source of comfort to certain Canadian boys to know that the bullet which maimed them for life was made from Canadian nickel sold by the International Nickel Company? To citizens of Vancouver it may be a source of patriotic pride to know that one of the Japanese bombing machines which bombed that city was manufactured by the Canadian

Foreign Policy-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
Car and Foundry Company and exported from this country on the 11th of February, 1938. If the Canadian people ever come to realize that concerns in this country, such as International Nickel and certain aircraft manufacturers, are making millions of dollars out of war material which may very shortly be used to destroy Canadian citizens and Canadian property, I believe they will rise up in righteous indignation and demand that the government take some action in this regard.
I ask the government, therefore, to give serious consideration to an economic embargo on all war materials as the major contribution Canada can make towards collective peace. I think we will all agree with the statement made to congress last fall by the President of the United States, who said:
There are ways, apart from war, which democratic nations can take to restrain an aggressor.
I suggest that this is one of the ways this country can take to restrain international aggressors, and I believe it is our solemn duty to take that step. May I quote another statement from the North American continent. In Hansard for April 1, 1935, I find these words:
I think this country ought to declare that any nation which could be shown to have threatened the peace of the world by violating a pact of collective security should be denied any assistance in the shape of men or munitions, should be denied any assistance in the nature of food, should be denied any assistance through credit. Our country, small as it is, might well lay down a definite policy in that regard as expressing Canada's attitude toward any country which upon the facts being disclosed was found to be guilty of attempting to destroy wrhat otherwise might be collective security. If that example were followed by other parts of the British Empire, as I believe it would be, it would soon be followed by other parts of the world.
That statement was made in this house by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I concur in every word he uttered, and now, almost to a day four years after he made the statement, I am asking him to practice in office what he preached in opposition. Even though the statement was made on April 1st I cannot believe that he was April-fooling. I think he meant it; and although the difficulties are numerous, I am sure the chances would be well worth taking. I believe the difficulties could be surmounted, and the contribution to peace would be perhaps greater than could be achieved by the people of Canada in any other single way.
May I remind the house that New Zealand, a much smaller dominion lying in an exposed position in the Pacific has shown its strict adherence to the cause of peace by imposing
an embargo as a protest against Japan's invasion of central China. The United States, which is not a member of the League of Nations, aroused by the recent acts of aggression on the part of Herr Hitler, has imposed a twenty-five per cent supertax on German exports to the United States. I would further remind the house that in 1937 this parliament stopped all shipments of war materials to Spain. If an embargo on shipments to Spain, a nation that was a friendly power and did not commit any acts of aggression, was justifiable, how much more justifiable ought an embargo to be against nations that have embarked upon a course of international piracy?
I direct the attention of the house to the recent plea by the London Financial News for a ban by the democratic countries on war materials to Germany. I quote from a Canadian Press dispatch dated London, March 29:
Marshalling of the peace-minded nations of the world into an economic bloc against the exportation to aggressor nations of raw materials essentia] for arms expansion was advocated editorially Tuesday by the Financial Neics.
Urging Great Britain to take the lead in effecting the embargo, the paper declared, with the cooperation of the United States and some smaller countries, a high percentage of most vital commodities could be withheld from powers threatening the world's peace.
"Surely it should be possible (quite apart from the question of political alliance) for the pacific nations to ensure it is not from their resources that these commodities-the raw materials of aggression-are drawn," the Financial Fetes said.
The paper cited Canada's position with regard to nickel exports.
As producer of 90 per cent of the world's nickel, it pointed out Canada last year supplied three-quarters of Germany's requirements. Con-' siderable inconvenience, the paper said, would be caused Germany by cutting off these supplies. but it was equally obvious a mere embargo of Canadian exports would prove futile.
The editorial proceeded that "to make the scheme reasonably effective it would be necessary in some cases to secure the cooperation of smaller countries, notably Holland and Belgium. This in turn would raise problems of compensation and perhaps involve political guarantees.
"It is clear that the difficulties are great and at this stage the more simple method might well be to cut off Germany's purchases at the source-by boycotting German exports and so reducing her foreign exchange.
"No doubt strong action will be opposed in official circles on the ground that it might provoke further aggression. This not only ignores the fact that as yet Germany has shown no need for provocation. It begs the fundamental issue at stake: can we muster courage, intelligence and the will to stop aggression?"
Where does Canada stand in relation to such a plea? Will the Prime Minister signify to the world that Canada is willing to make
2522	COMMONS
Foreign Policy-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
that contribution which she is best able to make, namely an economic contribution? Will he tell the world that Canada is prepared to see that, so far as we are able, not one ton of war materials will go from Canada into the hands of unscrupulous warmongers for the making of implements of death? I know that as a small nation, located on the north American continent, we are not a mighty factor in European affairs. There are times when our moral indignation wells up within us, when we think of the two million casualties that have taken place in China in the past year and a half. We have no power to stop the Japanese from killing the Chinese, but I do say, sir, that we have the power, so far as lies within us, to see that the Japanese do not get Canadian nickel and Canadian war materials with which to carry on their bloody and barbarous business. We have no power to stop Hitler's steam roller from rolling over Europe, crushing the small democracies that are in its way, but we have the power to see that, so far as within us lies, we prevent our potential sources of raw material from being used to build a mighty war machine.
The other day, when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was speaking, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) asked, "What are you going to do when there is a mad dog in Europe?" I quite agree, Mr. Speaker, that there is a mad dog in Europe, but I submit for the consideration of this house that we gave that mad dog teeth. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) said Hitler was a madman. Again I agree, but a madman is only dangerous when he has arms, and in our small way we have helped to see that he has arms. I rather blushed last winter when on Sunday evenings over the radio I heard prominent Canadians, good Christian people who were well inten-tioned, making an appeal for the Chinese Red Cross. It was a worthy cause, but I could not help realizing that at the same time that we were asking for funds to bind up China's wounds we were shipping aluminum, nickel, copper and scrap iron at the rate of a million dollars' worth a month out of Canada for Japan. That, to me, comes very close to hypocrisy.
I ask the government this question: What does it propose to do about the matter? Here is something we can do. Here is something that is not academic. Here is something that is not in the realm of speculation. Here is something that the Canadian people can do, and something to which the Prime Minister himself in 1935 gave his blessing. What do we propose to do about it? Is it possible that

we are not doing anything about it, because we are afraid we will interfere with the profits of those who benefit by this business? If that be true, then indeed this is a black day in Canada's history.
At this season of the year we draw close to Good Friday. All the eyes of the world will turn back to "a green hill far away, without a city wall," where the founder of Christianity was crucified by those forces of selfishness, greed, and lust for gain that are still at work in the world. It seems to me that unless we do something in Canada about the question of the export of war materials there will be another crucifixion-the crucifixion of a generation of young men, crucified upon a cross of nickel.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the speeches in this debate. Naturally in a time of world unrest, and especially a time such as that through which the world is now passing, an expression of opinion from parliamentarians who are interested is called for. Such expressions of opinion may set forth a wide and broad field of generalities. I listened with much interest to the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as he laid the foundation upon which he could express the foreign policy of his government. I should like to make a few observations with regard to that speech.
Perhaps what I have to say might best be said under three distinct headings: first, the right of parliament to decide such important issues as might involve the nation in armed conflict; second, the government's foreign policy with respect to trade agreements as a means of solving world problems and promoting better understanding to bring about international peace; and, third, if time permits, the pronouncement of the Prime Minister to the effect that in the event of war an armed force would be raised by volunteers and not by conscription.
With respect to the first point, namely that parliament must decide on these great issues, may I point out that a little while ago on this question the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) delivered a scholarly and well defined speech. As he was speaking, however, I did think there was some confusion in his use of the expressions "Canada and the Canadian people must decide", "parliament must decide", "the ministers of the crown must decide" and like terms. We need a definite understanding of what is meant by the assertion that parliament itself must decide, and I doubt whether to-day we have that understanding.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Hansell
The Prime Minister has made several pronouncements along that line which I shall take the liberty of reading. On March 20 of this year, in the course of a statement respecting the European crises, the Prime Minister said this, as reported at page 2043 of Hansard:
Canada at all times has been prepared to consult, as occasion might arise, with other freedom loving countries as to the most effective means of cooperation against aggression. The form of such cooperation and the contingency in which it may arise, are questions which this government will examine, in consultation with other governments. It will report its findings and any proposals that may result to this parliament, which has the sole and responsible authority to speak for Canada in such grave issues. I still believe in parliament as the most important of our national institutions; and in the supremacy otf parliament, especially where the issue is one of peace or war.
So far so good. On March 30 the Prime Minister was referring to Sir Wilfrid Laurier's stand in relation to England and Canada being at war, and he said this, as reported at page 2423 of Hansard:
My immediate purpose in quoting the statement,-
Of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

as will be apparent from the context, was to emphasize the continuity of Liberal policy as regards parliamentary control, the view which was held then and which we as a government hold to-day, that in the great as in the small issues of a nation's policy, the policy of selfgovernment which we have followed for a century makes it essential that parliament and no other body should decide.
From the same speech I quote the following, as reported at page 2418 of Hansard'.
If Canada is faced by the necessity of making a decision on the most serious and momentous issue that can face a nation, whether or not to take part in war, the principle of responsible government which has been our guide and our goal for a century past, demands that that decision be made by the parliament of Canada. Equally, the system of government we have inherited from Britain, of the close and essential relations between the legislature and the executive, makes it the duty of the government to propose to parliament the course which in regard to particular issues it considers should be adopted, and to stand or fall by the decision.
That is all very well and good. But the Prime Minister went on to speak concerning his pronouncement made at Geneva some little while ago. I quote from page 2418 of Hansard'.
Speaking as the Prime Minister of Canada, I wish to say that I am not prepared any more than is the Prime Minister of Great Britain to engage this country by new and unspecified commitments operating under conditions which cannot now be foreseen.
Panada's attitude as to automatic commitments involving possible or actual participation in war has been asserted time and again
both in this parliament and at Geneva. Whether it has been in reference to the application of sanctions under Article 16 of the covenant of the league or to participation in wars apart altogether from the league, Canada's position has been the same, namely, that in either case the approval of parliament will be required.
I should like to call the attention of hon. members to that little phrase which to my mind is very significant-"Canada's position has been the same, namely, that in either case the approval of parliament will be required." My contention is that there is a tremendous difference between parliament's deciding these momentous issues and parliament's simply approving of decisions which have already been made by the ministers of the crown or the governor in council. In support of this contention I should like to review briefly what took place immediately prior to the last war. I have here the official record as published in the volumes entitled Official History of the Canadian Forces in the Great War, 1914-1919 issued by authority of the Minister of National Defence. On page 7 of the first volume we read of what took place almost on the eve of the last war, and I want to show that parliament in the special war session-I think the newspapers called it that-was not called to meet until the 18th of August. Yet on the fourth of August, and previous to that, Canada had already taken steps to take part in any possible emergency that might arise. On the first of August the governor general of that day sent this message to the Secretary of State for the Colonies:
Urgent. My government desire me to send you the following:	"My advisers while expressing their most earnest hope that peaceful solution of existing international difficulties may be achieved and their strong desire to cooperate in every possible way for that purpose, wish me to convey to his majesty's government the firm assurance that if unhappily war should ensue the Canadian people will be united in a common resolve to put forth every effort to make every sacrifice necessary to ensure the integrity and maintain the honour of our empire."
Arthur.
That was on the first of August. The next day another cablegram was sent by the governor general, and signed Arthur, from which to save time I quote only this sentence:
They are confident that a considerable force would be available for service abroad.
That cablegram was sent on the second of August, two days before war was actually declared. Further, on the eve of war, His Majesty King George V sent a cablegram expressing his appreciation of the dominion's offer of cooperation at that particular time.
Foreign Policy-Mr. Hansell

On the fourth of August, when hope could no longer be entertained in London that war might be averted, the Secretary of State cabled that:
Though there seemed to be no immediate necessity for an expeditionary force from Canada, he thought it would be wise to take steps by which such a force could be provided in case it should be required later.
I believe that is a repetition of the actual words of the cablegram that was sent.
Acceptance of the offer of a Canadian military force was received in a cablegram dated August 6, from Harcourt, the Secretary of State for the Colonies:
His majesty's government gratefully accept your offer to send expeditionary force to this country, and would be glad if it could be despatched as soon as possible.
What I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, is that all these things were being done, even to the extent of committing Canada to raise an army for service overseas, before war was declared, and before parliament could possibly have been summoned. Parliament did not meet until August 18, 1914.
I am very glad that the Prime Minister has made a pronouncement along this line. But what happened in 1914 was this. When parliament met, commitments had already been made and parliament was expected simply to approve and ratify or disapprove the decisions that had already been made. I think the Prime Minister should point out very clearly just what is the position at the present time. Will parliament be called to ratify decisions already made, or will parliament be called to decide what shall be done? Of course conditions to-day are a little different from what they were in 1914. Parliament could not meet so quickly in 1914 as it could to-day, because our present air transportation facilities would permit of parliament meeting within twenty-four hours of being summoned. I trust the Prime Minister will make some further statement along this line.
The second observation I desire to make has to do with the government's foreign policy and with trade agreements as a means of contributing towards world peace. Speaking on the Canada-United States trade agreement some time ago, the Prime Minister said, as reported at pages 910 and 911 of Hansard:
The making of these agreements, especially when the world situation is so precarious as it unfortunately is, is an achievement of superlative importance, which will have its repercussions throughout the world in the next generation. In the present, each of us sleeps
[Mr. Hansell.)
more safely in his bed because of the rapprochement between the world's two greatest democracies, a rapprochement that could not have been effected without the assent and the cooperation of Canada.
Speaking on March 30 of the foreign policies of the government, the Prime Minister said, as reported on page 2419 of Hansard:
We have been considering at length this session, as we did at the first session of the present parliament, one of the most notable and practical evidences of that new understanding, the new trade agreement with the United States. I shall not do more than refer to- that achievement as one of the main objectives of our foreign policy, a definite contribution to stability and goodwill.
That is fine, but let me point out that this particular agreement is one with a peaceful and friendly nation. I have no quarrel with the contention that a better understanding can be brought about through proper reciprocal agreements between nations, but I believe the government owes it to parliament to say just what the government has done about negotiating trade agreements with these potential enemies whose voices shake the world. We know very little about that. A few years ago a grave situation arose through Mussolini's campaign of aggression in Ethiopia. Most of us would have liked to know more about the underlying situation. I think we should be told whether friendly negotiations looking to an increase in trade were carried on at that time.

Then there is the Spanish situation, where the developments were somewhat similar if not exactly parallel. Or consider the case of Germany. I discovered that in 1937 Germany had a favourable balance of trade of about 443,000,000 marks, whereas the next year her adverse balance amounted to
432,000,000 marks. We should be told what the government has done about establishing friendly trade relations with Germany. In saying that, I am not presenting a case for Germany; I think the fuehrer of Germany is well able to present his own. But I think we should know whether the government has done anything calculated to help towards lessening international friction by bringing about a little better understanding. Unquestionably the reason for the aggression of these dictator-ridden nations is economic. Italy, for instance, had to have certain raw materials, and the attitude of the people of that country seemed to be, "If the nations of the world will not give them to us we will take them." Last September, while the world was going through a serious crisis, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) was called home

Foreign Policy-Mr. Hansell
from Germany. We have not heard as to what negotiations he was able to carry on there. I think we should know. A few weeks ago the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston) asked a question of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley). It had been reported that Germany was willing to barter some of her machinery for Canadian wheat. The Minister of National Revenue replied that such an offer had been made. We have not heard anything about it since, and we should know what is being done. There is so much that we do not know.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) and I are used to arguing at home. We happen to live together in Ottawa. That is the reason for the little exchange. There are so many things covered up that probably nine out of ten members of parliament do not know what these underlying and fundamental influences are.
The Prime Minister stated that the government is opposed to conscripting any army to send to foreign shores. I agree with that point of view. I would make this observation, that should war break out and should the British isles be in danger of attack-as suggested last night on the air by a certain gentleman from Edmonton, clack-clacking away over a local station about this and that, depicting the possibility, for instance, of London being attacked by bombers-Canada would have no difficulty in raising a volunteer force. But should Great Britain be drawn into some international conflict involving military operations on the boundaries of southeastern Europe, the raising of a volunteer force in Canada might present some difficulties; in such an event we should ask, what are we fighting for?
There are some things which the British people hold very dear. We cherish our liberties. We like to think that ours is a
nation with liberties to protect. But the raising of armies to protect British financial interests in some other part of the world is a different matter. We are entitled to know the circumstances, and sometimes it is hard to discover them. I am certain that international complications arise because of financial interests being in conflict with one another in various parts of the world.
I am now going to digress for a little while to another subject. In this and in previous debates there has been a good deal of talk about the government making some particular pronouncement during the crisis last September. I am in hearty sympathy with the government for refraining to make a particular pronouncement at that particular time. Subsequent events have proved, I believe, that it was the wise thing for the Prime Minister not to make a special declaration then. Perhaps, however, we are in danger of pronouncements being made from other sources, unauthoritative sources, pronouncements not with regard to Canada's position but with regard to what should or should not be done. During the crisis just a couple of weeks ago, on a Saturday afternoon it was rumoured round the halls of this building that parliament might be called on the Sunday. As it happened, I had to go away on Sunday morning. In the station I bought a Toronto newspaper. Unfortunately. I did not take notice, when I cut out the article in which I was particularly interested, what newspaper it was. At any rate I read in that clipping an account of a meeting that was held by the Galt Women's Conservative Association "last night"-this is dated March 18. The article is headed:
Avoid shame of September Canada urged.
The sub-title reads:
Captain Rawson calls on King and Manion to pledge full support of dominion to Britain.
That is not so bad, but this is what I really take exception to. I have a strong feeling for the Prime Minister and others who are in authority in these matters. I recognize the extreme difficulty of their situation when they are called upon to make decisions, to know just what to do in such crises, because unquestionably such decisions call for the very best wisdom. At that time I read the following in this article:
Galt, March 18-"Last September Canadians hung their heads in shame through the shameful silence which resounded with a dull thud throughout the chancelleries of Europe"-
That is quite a statement.
-Captain Norman Rawson of Hamilton told the Galt Women's Conservative Association last night.
Foreign Policy-Mr. Hansell

I am going to suggest that this very gentleman is doing the thing which he labels as criminal; he is making a political football out of the situation. People should be careful what they say at these times. I do not know that I have a tremendous amount of confidence in any government to decide the right policy, but there is one thing I do stand for and it is this. The government when trying to do their best in time of international crises should have the common sympathy of men in responsible positions.
I trust that in the course of this debate we shall hear these questions answered: First, do we understand that parliament is to be called, in case of necessity, to decide the great issue, or is it going to be called to approve a decision that has already been made?
