speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 17, 1916, Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated:
There must be no conscription.
On the same date, January 17, 1916, Sir Robert Borden stated:
I made it clear to the Canadian people that we did not propose any conscription. I repeat that announcement to-day with emphasis.
A few months later, that is on May 18 of the same year,-which shows how quickly things change when a country is at war and has decided to take part, if only by the despatch of volunteers-I quote Mr. Henri Bourassa:
In his speech of May 18th Sir Robert Borden gave no serious justification for his change of front. He spoke with apparently sincere emotion of the losses suffered by the Canadian army; he said that unless we send reinforcements the number of Canadian soldiers in the trenches will diminish. That is obvious. The longer the war, the greater the losses; and if casualties are not replaced, the army will certainly diminish. But the Prime Minister knew that on January 17th, 1916, when he repeated with emphasis the announcement that there would be no conscription.
He added that voluntary enlistment was no longer giving tangible results. That also, everybody knew. It had long been demonstrated when, in Dorchester, Messrs. Sevigny and Blondiu swore to high heaven that conscription would never be voted. Voluntary enlistment had dried up when L'Evenement asserted, on behalf of the ministers and under their inspiration, that with the Conservative government there would never be conscription.
Sir Robert Borden was then appealing to Sir Wilfrid Laurier to join him in the government. Sir Wilfrid refused and most of his English Liberal friends from the other provinces separated from him in order to enter the Union government. A few of them, however, remained faithful to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and among these few was a man whose great name will live in history- the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, to-day leader of the government.
The war ended. Sir Wilfrid Laurier died and at the great convention organized to choose his successor, and at which I was a delegate, Mr. Fielding, whose name was proposed, was put aside because he had abandoned Laurier on the question of conscription, and the man who to-day leads the government was chosen. I can truthfully say that subsequent developments justified the attitude of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and of Mr. King, since at the election of December, 1921, the Liberal party, under the direction of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, came back to power.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Lacroix
The other day, I listened attentively to the following statement which the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made with regard to conscription:
So long as the Liberal government headed by Mackenzie King enjoys the confidence of parliament, young Canadians shall not be conscripted for overseas service.
I have every confidence in my leader, King, but I am convinced that should parliament decide to participate and start to dispatch volunteer forces to Europe, in the event of war lasting for any considerable time, there would be a repetition of what Sir Robert Borden said on the 18th May, 1916:
The longer war lasts, and the heavier the losses are without the casualties being made good, then it is clear that the army is dwindling.
I am convinced that England will tell us the very things that Sir Robert Borden conveyed to the Canadian people on the 18th May, 1916. As happened to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King will then cease to lead the government, a union cabinet will be formed, conscription will be enforced with the consent of parliament, and notwithstanding our regret at the departure of Mackenzie King, the trick will have 'been turned by the Imperialists of this country. This will come as a consequence of parliament deciding through a new so-called "union" government, to raise, at the expense of the Canadian government, a volunteer expeditionary force.
Let me frankly say that, in view of the stand previously taken and the statements already made by the Right Hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and considering his influence in the government, I am confident that no volunteer expeditionary force paid for and equipped by the Canadian government will ever leave our shores, so long as the King-Lapointe government is in power.
As a matter of fact, at a meeting held in Saint-Flavien, Lotbiniere county, on Sunday the 19th December, 1937, the right hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) spoke the following words about armaments as reported by Le Soleil on the 20th December of the same year:
We do not advocate sending any one to war. Let me repeat here this afternoon what I said from the floor of the Canadian parliament: each and every one of these expenses is made solely and exclusively for the defence of Canada.
I am convinced that if we were to assert definitely our right to neutrality, as it was irrefutably set forth by that prominent liberal, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson), who is a professor in the Manitoba Law
School, we would never have conscription in this country, unless we were attacked. And why should we not have the right to assert that principle and to wait at least until we know what action the United States would take? Is not Canada a part of America? The United States did not sign the last pact whereby England and France undertook to defend Poland. Are we going to fight for Danzig, which belonged to Germany before the great war?
The United States who entered the last war only a few months before its end and were thus spared the enormous expenditures which resulted from our automatic participation at the very beginning thereof, profited by a tremendous trade expansion during that whole period whereas we, with our small population, lost 60,000 men at the front and are still burdened, as the result of this automatic participation, with a debt of about 4 billion dollars. Why not reserve judgment and strongly assert that we too are entitled to determine the moment of our participation, which should not antedate that chosen by the United States.
During the last war, the United States remained neutral for quite a number of years, yet thousands upon thousands of Americans enlisted abroad. The British and French governments paid their travelling expenses and this enlistment was effected in France and in England, but not on American soil. I have no objection to any such enlistment in the next war, provided it is done under the same conditions.
In order to express the true feelings of all French-Canadians in this regard, I would like to read to you an excerpt from an article which was published in the Quebec Liberal Party's organ, Le Soleil, on Friday, March 31, 1939, under the title:	"No conscription,
but . .
Should England some day be in need of assistance, we shall undoubtedly see large numbers of young Canadians hasten to the aid of their mother country. Their example will even be followed by a lesser number of Canadians of French or foreign origin whose British feelings will be all the stronger that Great Britain will respect their country's right to self-determination. It would be the part of wisdom to leave such volunteers to be absorbed by the imperial army. Otherwise, should the national government organize Canadian contingents at its own expense, it would assume three serious responsibilities: firstly, that of taking a step likely to draw violent reprisals against Canada; secondly, that of engaging the credit of the nation in a ruinous undertaking; thirdly, that of accepting the logical or sentimental consequences of participation in a foreign war.
In 1914, it will be recalled, Sir Robert Borden's Tory government stated that voluntary enlistments would suffice to levy and maintain

Foreign Policy-Mr. Lacroix
the expeditionary force promised to England. In reply to direct questions, Sir Robert stated that he did not believe his government would ever have to resort to conscription. He repeated this indefinite statement on the morrow of the United States' entry in the European furnace in 1917. A few months later, however, he imposed compulsory military service on the youth of Canada, under the pretext that honour demanded that our volunteers be supported by all the human and material resources of the nation. The consequences of an ambiguous phrase came near disrupting Canadian unity for ever and causing civil war. A repetition of that mistake and deception must be avoided at all costs.
The United States, who remained neutral for several years during the great war, sold their goods to France, England and Russia, and enjoyed unparalleled prosperity while keeping at the same time out of debt. It would be useless to deny that English, French and American ships continuously carried armaments, munitions, and food to war-torn Europe, for several years, and that but for the Lusitania incident, the United States would probably never have entered the conflict.
In spite of their neutrality, the United States never prevented a foreign ship, even though she might be the Empress of Britain from loading cargoes in their sea ports during the time they were neutral. Their participation coming only towards the end of the war, their people were spared all the hardships Canada experienced during the great war. Why could not our country do the same thing, seeing that it is an American country and that the Statute of Westminster has given us our complete independence, whatever may be said to the contrary?
I would have voted without protesting, indeed with enthusiasm, all the millions that would have been asked, had I been given a legal guarantee that those millions would not have been used in order to send an expeditionary force overseas.
Ever since the military votes have been gradually increased each year, I have protested against such increases, because we had no guarantee such as I have mentioned, that is to say an assurance that the increased votes would not be used for external war, and today, if I may judge by the discussions in this chamber, it seems to be agreed that, in case of war, it would be difficult to avoid sending on the battlefields more expeditionary forces, equipped and armed at the expense of the Canadian government.
Well, sir, I desire to say without hesitation, as I have said every year since I have been a member of this house, that I will vote, when the house is asked to express its opinion, against any participation in foreign wars, knowing very well that, once we have decided to send

to Europe battalions of volunteers equipped at the expense of the Canadian government, history will necessarily repeat itself, as can be seen by the attitude of the Union government headed by Sir Robert Borden.
The same thing will occur again, I say, and, under colour of reinforcing the battalions of volunteers already in the line of action, it will be decided to impose conscription in this country.
I represent a constituency where I was elected, at the last general election, because I expressed myself as being opposed to any participation in foreign wars. I was an officer of the Quebec Anticonscription League which fought against conscription in 1916-17; I even travelled throughout the province of Quebec denouncing conscription; I always have advocated that policy and to-day I want to state it categorically in this chamber. I respect the opinion of my fellow members, but I could not do better than to repeat the following words of the former member for Labelle, Mr. Henri Bourassa, on the attitude of the French Canadians during the Great War:
But so long as the enlistment of soldiers remained nominally voluntary, they kept quiet. I believe it was a mistake. Once they thought the line had been overstepped and that the future of the country was endangered, they ought to have multiplied their public protests. They find their excuse in their extraordinary respect for the liberty of others. And they have so often been told not to speak aloud, nor to be the first to speak! They have been told so many times that conscription would never be voted nor even proposed!
When the statement of the Prime Minister dispelled every delusion and broke the promises of all representatives of the province of Quebec in the cabinet-even those of Sir Robert Borden himself,-the first reaction -was one of amazement; the second feeling was anger; the third was the unflinching determination to oppose such a tyrannical measure by every means of legitimate resistance.
It is useless to disguise the truth: there are two million French-Canadians who are flatly opposed to conscription. The few exceptions that may be found do not change the opinion of the majority; the half-hearted declarations which may be extorted, here and there, on the loyalist feelings of right-minded French-Canadians will only stiffen and exasperate this mass opposition.
And I may add, after quoting these words of Mr. Henri Bourassa, that to-day there are almost three million French-Canadians opposed to the sending abroad of an expeditionary force armed and equipped Iby the Canadian government, because they have learned the lesson of history.
Some of our people volunteered for service in the great war in the belief that this was a war to end war, they left of their own free

Foreign Policy-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
will, guided by an ideal which I respect, and I would like to salute " en passant " Mr. Speaker, the unpublicized heroism of those who fell at Yimy and Courcelette. They have undoubtedly written one of the greatest chapters of our history and I do not desire, for any reason, to belittle the magnificence of their gesture, but subsequent British governments who never understood the value of their sacrifice, resumed their balance of power policy in Europe by granting to Germany the concessions which enabled her to grow strong again; they are the true culprits whose political motto has always been: divide to govern.
And now, they would like to see our people return to European battlefields every twenty-five years, there to sacrifice our political future, since it must not be forgotten that the next war will foe longer than the last. We are afforded an example of this in Spain, a relatively small country, where the civil war lasted for more than three years. Shall we stand by and allow our country's future to be sacrificed once again and in a much more definite manner, without any advantages to be gained thereby?
Let us cease thinking as they do in London with regard to international relations and shift around a bit more to the point of view adopted in Washington.
I am certainly opposed to annexation of this country by the United States, but I would like to warn London that if they wish Canada to remain one of the brightest jewels of the British crown, they must cease requesting that we sacrifice on their behalf the very life blood of the nation in adventures which do not concern us; otherwise we are heading fatally towards independence. It is vital that the whole Canadian nation adopt the attitude held by the people of Quebec who are, notwithstanding assertions to the contrary, among the truest Canadians to foe found in the country.
Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, we shall be fatally drawn into all the conflicts which London is apt to encounter in all parts of the world, and I maintain that in order to be sure of the opinion of the Canadian people in the matter, it will be necessary to hold a referendum to the people on the subject of our participation in any foreign war, during the next general election or even before then, if possible.
A plebiscite is much more in keeping with the true principle of social order than electoral and parliamentary rule.
The former member for Labelle in the House of Commons, Mr. Henri Bourassa, had himself stated the necessity of a referendum on the subject, and this is what he said at the time:
At a general election, public opinion cannot express itself on a single issue; it is divided between the numerous problems which have been discussed in parliament or in public for many years; it has to give a decision on the varied problems which the next parliament will have to solve; and it is pulled on all sides by party ties, by personal sympathies for a leader or a candidate, by a thousand matters of local interest.
Each day brings us nearer to the possibility of participation in a war. We still have ample time to consult the public and I feel assured that the Canadian people would share our views on the subject.
Before closing my remarks, I want to challenge the statements of the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh). He dared to state that Canada is not a nation, and he went on to say that the speech delivered in this chamber, last Friday, by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe), did not represent the sentiment of the province of Quebec. Let not the hon. member deceive himself. The expression of the sentiment of his province will come very soon to awaken him from his colonial and imperialistic lethargy. The awakening will be the more unexpected and the more sudden for the hon. member that his sleep of colonialism will have been the sweeter.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this discussion seems to be concerned largely with what position Canada will take in case of war. I believe this is one of the most important questions which confront us at this time. I have read with a great deal of care the speech of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), but I must confess that as yet I have not been able to ascertain exactly what position we shall take in case war breaks out. It seems queer that we should permit any other country, no matter what country it may be, to commit us to war without Canada having some say in the matter. I have in my hand a copy of the Edmonton Journal of September 27, containing the text of a speech by Mr. Chamberlain, in which I find the following:
"If I were convinced that any nation had made up its mind to dominate the world by force I should not hesitate to resist it," the Prime Minister declared in a broadcast from 10 Downing street.
I notice that the emphasis is laid on the words "if I were convinced." I do not take issue with that statement, but from that phrase it seems to me that the issue depends upon one individual. It may be truly said that he represents the British government, but what right has the British government, through Mr. Chamberlain, to enter upon a war in
2530	COMMONS
Foreign Policy-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
which we might take part, while we have no say about the matter? In the same speech Mr. Chamberlain said:
"I find Herr Hitler's attitude unreasonable in his final demands," he continued. "But I shall not give up my hope for a peaceful solution." He declared: "We cannot undertake to involve the whole of the British empire in war however much we may sympathize with a small nation-if we have to fight it must be on larger issues than that."
When we look at this carefully, we find that he says, "We cannot undertake to involve the whole of the British empire in war." I believe it would seem to anyone reading or listening to that statement that the whole issue depended upon his decision, and that no matter how his decision might go, the whole of the British empire would be involved. That is a unique position for any individual to be in, and surely Canada should have an opportunity of deciding whether or not she would partake in any foreign war.
It has been said in the house that Canada will decide. It has been said, and I believe by the Prime Minister, that the legal position was not definitely known, that it was not clearly defined. That being the case, I would say that Mr. Chamberlain was quite correct in what he said, and that he could involve the whole of the British empire.
The Prime Minister quoted Sir Wilfrid Laurier's words as follows, at page 2423 of Hansard of this year:
If England is at war we are at war and liable to attack. I do not say that we shall always be attacked, neither do I say that we would take part in all the wars of England. That is a matter that must be guided by circumstances, upon which the Canadian parliament will have to pronounce and will have to decide in its own best judgment.
I am not exactly clear as to the meaning of those observations, especially when I compare them with those of the Prime Minister to the effect that Canada's attitude is subject to approval by parliament. When I think back to the time of the abdication of King Edward VIII, I remember distinctly the decision was made before parliament was called to give its approval. In view of that fact it would seem to me the Prime Minister's statement that Canada's attitude is subject to approval by parliament would mean that the government could commit the country, and then would call parliament to decide. We know enough about politics, from our short experience in the house, to know that parliament would decide in favour of the government's action, especially at a time when the government had the majority enjoyed by the present one. Otherwise they would lose their

jobs, or political pressure could be brought to bear upon them to have them agree with government policy.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We would all lose our jobs-the whole parliament.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a point I should like to have cleared in my mind. Would parliament be called before commitments were made, or in the event of a crisis arising would the government say that Canada is going to take part in a war, and have the stage all set before it called parliament to make a decision? I am not making these observations in any spirit of criticism of the Prime Minister, but I should like to have settled in my own mind the question whether parliament would be called before commitments were made, or whether it would not be called until after they had been made.
Probably a plebiscite would be more suitable in the event of a crisis.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How long would that
take?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With our present methods of news distribution I should think one or two weeks would be sufficient. Certainly it would not take longer than that. A crisis would not come on us so suddenly that we would not have two weeks to spare.
I am in accord with the statement made not long ago, I believe by the Prime Minister, that before Canada can remain neutral it must have a proper defence force. I have said on other occasions that our defences should be adequate, and I am still of that opinion. I do not believe we should sit back and await the protection of the United States. If we are to decide whether or not we shall take part in a war, then we should be in a position to participate to the best advantage in a war. Certainly we cannot do that if we have only a few of those little pop-guns on the Pacific coast. We should have a proper defence force and defence policy.
But, somebody says, " That will cost money." Well, suppose it does cost money; when people's lives are at stake, money should not be considered seriously. And, speaking of money, if there is anything I deplore it is profiteering in war materials. The Prime Minister aptly referred to blood-money. Referring to profits on war supplies the Prime Minister is reported at page 2426 of Hansard as follows:
One political fact is equally clear: In a war to save the liberty of others, and thus our own, we should not sacrifice our own liberty or our own unity.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
With that I am fully in accord.
Planning and coordination would be essential, but the necessary coordination could be made, and if this government were in power-
And I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that it is in power with one of the greatest majorities it ever had, or ever will have.
-it would be made, without sacrificing those vital ends and conditions of our existence.
And this is the part with which I am particularly concerned:
Profits could and would be rigidly controlled

With the emphasis on " could and would."
-and profiteering suppressed. But men's lives and men's wills cannot be put on the same basis as goods and profits.
It would seem from some of the facts which have been disclosed in connection with the Bren gun contract, and some information revealed in regard to other contracts, where there was a five per cent limit on profits, that there is room for some consideration of this question. I 'believe some people in Canada are under the impression that from now on only five per cent profits will be made. Yet we have learned in the house that this provision applies to only a very small proportion of the contracts. On the others extremely large profits will be made.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before six o'clock I had referred to a passage from the Prime Minister's speech in which he said that " profits could and would be rigidly controlled, and profiteering suppressed." That was when war broke out. But it was most clear, I said, that profiteering was going on at the present time. One would infer that the Prime Minister himself was well aware of that fact when he stressed that, should war break out, profits could and would be rigidly controlled. But instead of waiting until these huge profits, or blood-money as the Prime Minister so aptly described them, have been accumulated, it seems to me that now is the proper time to curtail them; and that should not be an impossibility because, to use the Prime Minister's own words again, these profits could and would be controlled. It is no use trying to camouflage the thing and passing out propaganda that we are now, through the creation of the defence purchasing board, controlling profits in the manufacture of munitions. By that legislation we have said
that profits shall foe limited to five per cent, *but anyone who knows anything about it knows that the five per cent limitation applies to only a small proportion of the contracts to foe let. Also, there are other ways in which profits can be made. I have a clipping here from the Calgary Albertan of November 17, 1938, describing certain conditions which I was very much surprised to think could possibly exist. It says:
There is nothing spectacular in our commonplace British souls and whenever we try to stage-manage anything it is sure to come a cropper. You recall the dream of the Munich telegram which arrived at the conclusion of the Chamberlain speech following Godesberg which was ending in gloom and dismay. The Prime Minister took the telegram handed so dramatically from Halifax at the very right moment, read the message, "I have been invited by Herr Hitler to meet him in Munich." It needs only a sentimental Beverly Baxter to describe the sequel, the emotion, the applause, the turmoil, the "good old Nevilles," the tears that were shed by bucketfuls by strong men and such like.
What will you say to me or do to me if I tell you that it was all stage-managed and that the telegram had been received hours before and Chamberlain and quite a number of others knew of it?
"Critic," one of the editors of the New Statesman writes, "The Munich meeting was announced on the Italian radio Wednesday morning: I know a city man who received information in the morning from the private secretary of one of the members of the French cabinet that there would be no war and that he could make pots of money if he went ahead before Chamberlain's speech: the same information came over the 'phone in the morning from a big bank in Switzerland: and a good many people knew-I do not mean guessed-while Mr. Chamberlain was speaking that the speech was to end in peace and not war."
Another bit of drama gone to the scrap-heap. It pains me to say anything approving of the Hitlerites, but Goebbels could have managed it better than that.
If such conditions as those are to exist, it is beyond all reason. I do not say that is what actually took place, but I do say that under our present method of producing war supplies it might easily happen right here in Canada. We know beyond a doubt that during the last war there were many millionaires made here in Canada and they never became millionaires by going overseas and fighting for SI .10 a day. The Prime Minister says that when war breaks out, profits can and will be controlled. Why is it not done now? That is a question all Canadians are asking, and rightly so. Why should men be asked to go overseas and fight for SI.10 a day when others are permitted to make huge profits out of the manufacture of munitions? It is no good passing the thing off and saying: We will do it when war breaks out. Then it will be too late, for the profits will have been
2532	COMMONS
Foreign Policy-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
accumulated. Then we shall be waving the flag of patriotism and urging the ordinary man to go and fight for his country for $1.10 a day. Is it any wonder that a man came into my office the other day and said, when I asked him if he would fight in another war, "What for? I have no country to fight for. Canada does not even give me a job so that I can feed my wife and family." But we will wave the flag of patriotism in front of him to get him to fight for $1.10 a day, while large profits are being made by others from munitions. I say now is the time to control the profits. We should not wait until war breaks out and then have the Prime Minister say: "Profits will be controlled."

speechtext:
There is
a bill limiting profits to five per cent, but that limitation applies only to a very special kind of contract. If that legislation were broadened to cover the whole field of munitions production, I would say the Prime Minister was to be commended. He would certainly have my support if he made the declaration to-day that no profits over five per cent would be allowed in any shape or form of munitions contract, and I think this house would be one hundred per cent behind him. Why wait until it is too late?
I have received a number of letters and resolutions not only from my own constituency but from all over the country, asking for an embargo on the export of war materials, and may I say that I am in hearty accord with that course. I cannot for the life of me understand why last year-I have not checked up on it this year-the dominion

government issued something like 196 permits for the export of manufactured war materials. We send them not only to China but even to Japan, a country which we probably may be fighting some day. We send them to Germany and to the United States. Surely the United States does not need them. No, they are shipped in a roundabout way to different warring nations. I think it is only a fair and reasonable request, Mr. Speaker, that the government should place an embargo on manufactured war materials including the exportation of copper, nickel and other metals which go into their manufacture. Why, we are even exporting scrapiron right now, which without any trouble can be put into munitions to blow us all to pieces. And we call that sound financing of war!
I said before the house rose at six o'clock that we should have a proper defence for this country, and I am quite convinced of that. We should have an adequate defence. But the question of financing the manufacture of armaments must be settled soon. I cannot see how this nation can go on continually destroying the substance of our country and ever expect to get out of the dilemma in which we find ourselves. Great Britain has already announced that her taxes will be increased to provide for her armament program. Her armaments estimates have doubled and trebled, and now they are talking in billions for armaments. Here in Canada last year our defence estimates amounted to $35,000,000, and this year it is $65,000,000, or just about double.
It was aptly said the other evening by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) that if war broke out, new methods would be found overnight for financing the war. Apparently we can find money for that purpose, if for nothing else. Where is this mad race going to lead us? Continually we borrow money, increase the national debt and increase taxes. Surely there must be some conclusion to this, some end reached, unless we are to accept the attitude expressed the other day by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) when he said in effect, "Why worry about the national debt; coming generations will find some method of solving that trouble and we need not bother about it. Maybe that is the proper method; maybe it is the sound and logical course, when we are sitting pasv sively on the brink of war. But to my mind this whole business testifies to the bankruptcy of modern politics. Politics must be changed; if we are to get an}rwhere in building up the defence of Canada a new system must be found. I venture to say that if the

Foreign Policy-Mr. MacNeil
onus were put upon the Bank of Canada to finance this defence program without increasing either taxation or the national debt they would do it, because I believe we in Canada have sufficient brains-if we have not, God help us-to find some new method whereby this financing can be done.
It is a foregone conclusion that we shall be asked-indeed, we are being asked-to finance the whole program on borrowed money. We are going to increase the national debt by leaps and bounds. We are going to heap more taxes upon the people, -which means necessarily a lower standard of living, resulting in increased unemployment and intensified dissatisfaction, all of which will by no means tend to that national unity of which we hear so much. Surely if there ever were a time when unity was needed, it is now. If, as has been so often declared in this chamber, the present is a national emergency, why not face the facts as they are? Why not order the Bank of Canada to do something about the matter, and then let the Prime Minister put into effect his promise, made in 1935, that he was going to issue currency and credit in terms of public need. Surely the defence of our country, when the very lives of our citizens depend upon it, is a national emergency, and if ever there were a time when it was needful to have money issued in terms of public need, and not borrowed, now is the time; we should not wait to do it until we get into a war. On the old system of "sound" finance we could not finance another war if we tried to, we would be bankrupt in no time. As the Minister of Finance said, other means would have to be found overnight.
Let us look at the situation in some other countries. Whether we like it or not, we should fairly and squarely ask ourselves; How did Germany manage to get into the position she now holds? After 1918 she was the most downtrodden nation in existence. To-day she ranks among the greatest powers in the world. Did she accomplish all this by "sound" finance? I hardly think so. No nation would give her credit, no nation would even trade with her. She was forced to operate on a new system, and she did it most effectively, so much so that we in Canada and people in other countries are wondering how it came about. If we have not now the intelligence to stop and consider how Germany was able to achieve her present position, then there must be something wrong with us mentally because before long we shall have to look these facts in the face. How did Italy conquer Ethiopia? Was it done on "sound" finance? I think not. These are considerations which are facing us
directly; here are problems which, sooner or later, we must settle.
We possess in this country all the things we require for a proper, adequate and efficient defence. Canada is considered to be one of the richest countries in the world in respect of natural resources, including materials which can be converted into weapons of war. There is no question that we have an unlimited supply of labour. There are thousands of unemployed walking the streets; ninety-nine per cent of them are only too eager to get employment; they would take a job at a moment's notice if they were given sufficient wages to keep their families. Thus we have material and labour in abundance. Surely we have the brains to bring them together; the only thing lacking seems to be money, which is just a means to an end, yet we are forever increasing the burdens on the people because we have not sufficient intelligence to sit down together and solve that one problem of money. When that is solved, the other difficulties will rectify themselves. We could build a wonderful defence system in this country. If we have arrived at a position where it is necessary for us to arm-and that seems to be the opinion of some-we cannot be hampered by those who sit in control of money; we must set aside their opposition and see to it that every possible means is used, and we can build in this country a defence second to none without increasing the taxes or adding to the burdens of our people. Until such time as that is done-and the present time is, I think, most opportune-we shall never have a really united Canada.

speechtext:
In opening this debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to the desirability of maintaining unity in Canada, and also referred to the circumstances under which the Canadian people were being made aware of world trends and the effect of world trends on the security of Canada. The tragic feature of the situation, in view of the stimulus which has been given to public thinking in this regard, is that all efforts to determine and give expression to public opinion are in vain; for Canada has not yet claimed the right to determine its own foreign policy. I consider that we are now without a clear-cut foreign policy very largely because we have not asserted our legal right, guaranteed to us in 1926, by which we might determine on our own behalf our own external relations.
Our constitutional difficulties were ably explained this afternoon and on a previous occasion by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson). I desire to congratulate him

Foreign Policy-Mr. MacNeil
warmly upon the contribution he has made to this debate. Whether hon. members agree with him or not, they must admit that he has brought our thinking into focus on this vital subject; and when I heard him this afternoon advance his views against the criticism that his point of view was merely academic and also might be construed as anti-British in character, I thought of the remarks of Professor Corbett, who takes a similar point of view, and to whom reference has already been made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). Professor Corbett, in a recent broadcast and in an attempt to define his approach to this subject, said;
All that I plead is that we shall not accept our ideas on these vital matters in ready-made, inherited patterns. I am no rebel; for if I assert the democratic right of sober, frank statement, I am content also to abide by that other rule of democracy which requires obedience to the majority when once it has declared itself. When I say this, I speak not as one who has only contemplated from an armchair the lengths to which such obedience may lead one. I speak as one who knows from intimate personal experience the ultimate requirements of citizenship.
Evidently Professor Corbett spoke as an ex-service man, as did the hon. member for Selkirk this afternoon. I am in accord with the principle of self-determination in these matters as enunciated by the hon. member for Selkirk, largely because it is democratic and is a sane and logical development of constitutional processes as they have evolved since the great war. Our status of nationhood is in very large measure on account of the fact that Canada participated in the great war.
I have another reason for supporting the principles advanced by the hon. member for Selkirk, and I find these also expressed in clear and lucid language by Professor Corbett in the same broadcast, in which he said:
As I see things, there has not since 1931 been any intelligent direction to British foreign policy. It is a series of haphazard expedients. That is why I no longer care to see this country involved willy-nilly in the devious course which Downing street pursues. ... It may be that the United Kingdom will never be involved in a war in which this country might not join with a whole heart and a clear conscience. But to my mind it is no longer right to take that for granted. The consequences-of Britain's present course are too hopelessly unpredictable.
Nor is it enough that, as everyone knows, we already have the right on paper to abstain from active participation. Passive belligerency is still a state of war and exposes us to all the measures of war taken by Britain's enemy. Freedom to be neutral in the full technical sense is what we need. Only so, when crisis comes, can we really decide for ourselves how far we shall allow ourselves to be involved.
Having that freedom we should be in a position really to influence the course of British action.

Such a position is entirely in accord with democratic principles. Much of the loyalty or patriotism I hear expressed is Simon-pure colonialism that belongs to a bygone era. We have acquired a certain status of nationhood and we should assert our legal rights with respect to that status. It is impossible for us to attempt to encourage democracy in one compartment of our national life and stifle it in another, and I consider it the very essence of democracy that we should assert our rights in this regard.
Some reference has been made to knight-errantry abroad in the name of democracy. I suggest that, if we are required to consider the possibilities of armed conflict abroad in the name of democracy, we should take special care that our democracy at home is not destroyed in the process. It is not compatible with my conception of democracy that we should sign a blank cheque for Downing street and later fill in the blank with Canadian lives. But at the moment I do not intend to follow the arguments of the hon. member for Selkirk, but will suggest other practical steps that should be taken at this time with regard to Canadian control over acts of participation in external war.
If, as the Prime Minister suggests, we should not regard war as inevitable but at the same time should prepare to defend ourselves against invasion, it is quite as logical that we should scrutinize with greater care than ever before the articles of war for Canada, the legal mechanism by which Canada may be involved in war. I might suggest a number of practical steps that may be taken at this time without jeopardizing in any way commonwealth relations or without offering any crumb of comfort to potential enemies.
I suggest that steps should be taken now to ensure that we have definite parliamentary control over the armed forces of the dominion, and that we should ensure by statute prior parliamentary sanction for any act of participation in external war or any commitment in regard thereto. I also suggest that by enactment we should restrict the power now vested in the governor general to impose compulsory military service on the male inhabitants of Canada and place authority for general compulsory mobilization solely with parliament. I think it would be well to examine the existing legislation constituting the articles of war for Canada. This legislation is found in the Militia Act of Canada, the Naval Service Act, and curiously enough, in the Army Act of Great Britain as well; for it is specified in the Militia Act of Canada that the Army Act of Great Britain shall have

Foreign Policy-Mr. MacNeil
the same force and effect in Canada as if it had been enacted by the parliament of Canada for the government of the militia.
The first point to which I wish to direct the attention of the house is that the command of the armed forces of this dominion is vested in the governor general. It is, of course, in accordance with the terms of the British North America Act that the command in chief of the armed forces should be vested in his majesty, but the Militia Act goes beyond that. It declares that the exercise of that authority shall be by his majesty or by the governor general as his representative. In the old act which existed prior to 1904 the word " personal " was used. It is noteworthy that the term governor general is used in this particular section, whereas in many other sections of the act the term " governor general in council " is used with regard to the exercise of such authority. It is also important to note that the preceding section relates to the Interpretation Act. It declares that the Interpretation Act shall apply to all regulations, orders and articles of engagement lawfully made under the Militia Act; and in the Interpretation Act a clear distinction is made between the governor general acting as the personal representative of his majesty and the governor general acting on the advice of his majesty's ministers in the dominion.
When this act was under discussion in 1904, parliament made very clear its intention with regard to the interpretation of this section. On that occasion parliament rejected an amendment which proposed that the prerogatives of the crown should be exercised only upon advice of his majesty's ministers in the dominion. At page 6403 of Hansard of July 11, 1904, Mr. Bourassa moved the following amendment, that the act should be amended to read:
The command in chief of the militia is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the king and shall be exercised and administered by the governor general in council.
That amendment was rejected by parliament at that time, leaving no doubt as to the intention that the prerogatives of the crown in this respect might be exercised by the governor general in person. Mr. Bourassa at that time said that the issue was whether parliament should declare that the control of the militia was vested in the governor general personally or in the Canadian government. He pointed out the danger that these words might be interpreted for purposes other than those for which they were intended, and he definitely referred to an interpretation of the law repeated in the presence of Lord Minto when acting as governor general of Canada four years previously, when it was declared in the 71492-160
presence of his excellency that he might on his own authority take personal command of the armed forces of the dominion. The late Sir Robert Borden in his memoirs refers to a definite conflict between himself and His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught on that issue. At that time his royal highness, acting as governor general, said his authority involved something more than merely nominal command of the armed forces of Canada.
The wording of the statute assumes importance when it is noted that the governor general and not the governor in council is given power to impose compulsory military service, and the Army Act of the United Kingdom is made applicable to the forces of the dominion.
This was brought out more clearly during the great war. I quote from the official war history in reference to the status of the Canadian expeditionary force. It says:
That the Canadian expeditionary force was offered by Canada, and raised by the governor general by order of his majesty the king, had been plain enough since August, 1914; not until September, 1916, was the status understood to be that of Canadian volunteer militia on active service, employed in defending their country abroad. Every member of the force had been previously enrolled in a unit of the militia, a term defined ever since 1904 in the Militia Act as embracing all the military forces of Canada. Each was separately attested in the Canadian expeditionary force, and was equipped and paid by the Canadian government in fulfilment of the implication of the simple two-party agreement then made between each man and King George V.
Clearly the terms of enlistment were a direct contract between each member of the Canadian expeditionary force and his majesty. That should be cleared up. I see no reason why, in view of the present constitutional status of Canada, we should not have in this important statute, which assumes increasing importance as the international tension increases, a clear cut declaration of the rights of the government of Canada with respect to control of the armed forces of the dominion. There should be no ambiguity on this point.
Moreover we should examine the Militia Act in the light of present-day events. The Militia Act to-day clearly states that all the male inhabitants of Canada between the ages of eighteen and sixty are liable to military service, unless exempt or disqualified by law.
Provided that the governor general-
And here it says the governor general, not the governor in council.
-may require all the male inhabitants of Canada capable of bearing arms, to serve in the case of a lev6e en masse.
For this purpose the act now declares that all the male inhabitants of Canada shall be

Foreign Policy-Mr. MacNeil
divided into four classes: first, single men between eighteen and thirty and widowers without children; second, those between thirty and forty-five being single or widowers without children, and so on. And it says that the said classes shall be called upon to serve in the order specified.
The act goes on to say that the active militia shall consist of corps raised by voluntary enlistment and corps raised by ballot. Provision is made that the governor in council may determine the necessary military establishment for Canada, and if that establishment cannot be brought up to strength by voluntary enlistment the governor in council has power to draft men by ballot. For that purpose the country is divided into military districts, and the district officer commanding may be authorized to take such steps as are necessary to draft men into the service. Full power to enact the required regulations in this respect is vested in the governor in council. A curious feature is that there is an obsolete provision in this statute, whereby a man may secure exemption from military service if he provides a satisfactory substitute. As the Army Act of Great Britain applies as though enacted by the parliament of Canada, it was contended during 1917 by eminent members of the legal profession that a man might purchase release from service upon payment of ten pounds sterling. The Army Act was referred to in the regulations only recently promulgated under the authority of order in council P.C. 2974, dated November 29, 1938, in respect of those regulations applying to the Canadian force for the enforcement of discipline. So it follows, I think, that the incorporation of the Army Act of Great Britain in the Militia Act of Canada confers power upon the military authorities to court-martial and shoot a man for desertion or cowardice or evasion of military duty. We know that under the Army Act Canadians were executed during the great war.
The sections relating to compulsory military service originated in the Militia Act, 1868, as introduced by Sir George Cartier. It was stated then that all the male inhabitants of Canada constituted the militia. That principle was modified to some extent in 1904 when it said that all the male inhabitants of Canada were liable to military service. This point was raised by Sir Robert Borden in 1917. Parliament in 1868 rejected an amendment proposing that the forces of the dominion should be recruited by voluntary enlistment. At that time the feature of compulsory military sendee on the French pattern was incorporated in the Canadian law and

has remained the law of the land to this day. This principle was referred to by Sir Robert Borden on the first reading of the Military Service Act in 1917. On that occasion he attempted to refute the charge that he had broken any promise previously made to the Canadian people that he would not impose compulsory military service in Canada. He also attempted to refute the charge that he was introducing the Military Service Act of 1917 at the dictation of the British government. -He referred to the principles incorporated in the act dating back to 1868, and the fact that on division parliament then rejected the amendment proposing voluntary enlistment in 1868, and he said this, which I think it is important to place on record at this time:
It must be apparent, therefore, that the whole question of compulsory service was taken into consideration by the founders of confederation in almost the first session of this parliament, and that then it was decided, once for all, that for the defence of this country, and whether within or out of Canada, the people of this country should be subject to compulsory military service. And this has remained the law of the country from the day it was enacted in 1868 and it is the law of the land to-day.
And he says further:
Now let us look for a moment at the provisions of the Militia Act, which was passed in its present form in 1904, and which is now known as chapter 41 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906.
And he quotes sections 10 and 69, to which I have referred, section 69 reading:
69. The governor in council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
Sir Robert Borden then said:
Hon. members will observe that there is a slight difference in the provisions of section 69 from the corresponding section of the act of 1868, that is, section 61. There was some debate in 1904 upon that change, and to this I will come a little later. Meantime I desire to point out that this enactment is based upon the principle, which is as old as the principle of self-government, that while the state owes to its citizens certain duties, the citizens also owes corresponding duties to the state. To the citizen the state assures protection and security of his person and property, the enforcement of law and orderly government. To the state each citizen owes a duty of service, and the highest duty of all is the obligation to assist in defending the rights, the institutions and the liberties of his country. I desire to express my profound conviction that there never has been, and there never will be, an occasion when that duty could be more manifest, more urgent, and more imperative than at the present time.

Foreign Policy-Mr. MacNeil
And he says:
It may be asked: Why is this law necessary if such provision already exists in the Militia Act?
He is referring to .the Military Service Act, 1917.
The answer is very simple. We have sent 326,000 men overseas in the Canadian expeditionary force besides those who have gone to serve in the allied armies. The Militia Act provides that the selection shall be by ballot and in no other way. The government is convinced that such a method of selection would be unwise and even disastrous, under present conditions and having regard to the number of men required. We propose not to change or enlarge the compulsory principle, but merely to provide that selection shall not be made by ballot, that is, by blind chance. We are convinced that the selection should be based upon an intelligent consideration of the country's needs and conditions.
On March 30, at page 2426 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
The present government believes that conscription of men for overseas service would not be a necessary or an effective step. Let me say that so long as this government may be in power, no such measure will be enacted.
I suggest that if the Prime Minister means what he says with regard to conscription or compulsory military service in Canada, he should during the present session of parliament take steps to amend the Militia Act and the Naval Service Act, and should introduce an Army Act for Canada in the right of the dominion that will make it clear that parliament has definite control over military service and acts of participation in external wars. The question to some extent relates to that introduced by the hon. member for Selkirk.
I should like to make one further point. There can be no doubt, I think, about the interpretation of the existing provisions of the Militia Act. That interpretation was made clear by the parliament of Canada in the preamble to the Military Service Act of 1917, which reads:
Whereas by section ten of the Militia Act, chapter forty-one of the revised statutes of Canada, 1906, it is enacted as follows:
"All the male inhabitants of Canada, of the age of eighteen years and upwards, and under sixty, not exempt or disqualified by law, and being British subjects, shall be liable to service in the militia:	Provided that the governor
general may require all the male inhabitants of Canada, capable of bearing arms, to serve in the case of a levee en masse;"
And whereas by section sixty-nine of the said act it is further enacted as follows:-
"The governor in council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency:"
And whereas by the said act it is further enacted that, if at any time enough men do not volunteer to complete the quota required, the men so liable to serve shall be drafted by ballot;
And whereas to maintain and support the Canadian expenditionary force now engaged in active service overseas for the defence and security of Canada, the preservation of the empire and of human liberty, it is necessary to provide reinforcements for such expeditionary force;
And whereas enough men do not volunteer to provide such reinforcements;
And whereas by reason of the large number of men who have already left agricultural and industrial pursuits in Canada to join such expeditionary force as volunteers . . .
Then it goes on to give further reasons for the enactment of the Military Service Act. We were informed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that this act lapsed at the conclusion of the great war; but the Militia Act of Canada is still in force, and if a war broke out to-morrow I' see no escape from this interpretation which has been placed upon that act by the parliament of Canada. Furthermore, the Naval Service Act now in force provides that the governor in council may place the naval services of Canada at the disposal of his majesty for general service with the royal navy. That also confers power upon the executive to engage or participate in acts of external warfare without reference to parliament.
It may seem that I am drawing the longbow in this matter, but I should like to take a few minutes to give the time-table of events that occurred in August, 1914, by which Canada was, under the legislation to which I have just referred, committed, without reference to parliament, on every essential point to participation in external war. On July 30 a special meeting of the militia council considered tentative preparations for a first contingent of 25,000 men overseas. On July 31 all military districts were warned to make plans for an overseas contingent. On August 1-and remember, war was declared on August 4, while parliament did not meet until August 18-the British government was assured that in the event of war Canada would make every sacrifice for the empire, and H.M.C.S. Rainbow was made available for the protection of trade routes. On August 2 a proposal was made to the British government to render aid in the event of war by sending Canadian units overseas. On the same day the Rainbow received orders from the admiralty to proceed south and guard the trade routes. On August 4 the governor general proclaimed that Canada was in a state of war. On the same date an order in council was passed under the authority of the Naval Service Act
Foreign Policy-Mr. MacNeil

of Canada placing the naval services of this country on active service and at the disposal of his majesty for service with the royal navy. On August 5 the Canadian militia, by order in council, were required to complete training under section 52 of the Militia Act. On the same date the Canadian government cabled the British government asking for an imperial order bringing Canadian volunteers under sections 175 and 176 of the Army Act, as provided in the Militia Act. On the same date the Rainbow received further orders, to which I shall refer later.
Then, on August 6, the British government cabled its acceptance of the offer of an expeditionary force and urged that it be dispatched as soon as possible. On the same date an order in council was passed authorizing the raising and equipping of militia units composed of officers and men willing to volunteer for service overseas under the British crown. On August 7 the British government cabled that one division would be a suitable composition for the expeditionary force. On August 9 a cable was received in Canada by the governor general, indicating that His Majesty the King had ordered "that the troops offered by Canada shall be raised by your royal highness for service as expeditionary force." On August 10 an order in council authorized the composition of an overseas expeditionary force. On August 11 the adjutant general instructed all officers commanding that volunteers for the overseas contingent must be enlisted immediately in the Canadian militia, enlistment in the contingent to be carried out at Valcartier. On August 15 the Minister of Militia speaking in Montreal said, "Canada is sending twenty thousand men to the front." Finally, on August 18 parliament met and in a few days passed the War Measures Act giving blanket ratification to all these steps already taken by the executive committing Canada to external war.

speechtext:
Parliament had no alternative but to accept as irrevocable the steps already taken by the executive.
Perhaps I may now take a few minutes to tell the story of the Rainbow, which had been stationed at Esquimalt. It had been practically out of commission; I think it had put to sea once, in March, 1913. On August 1 the Rainbow received orders to prepare to put to sea to guard the trade routes north of the equator. It was rumored that the Leipzig and the Niimberg were preparing to raid shipping in the Pacific. The commander of the Rainbow-and I think this is important- when he received these orders on the second

or third of August, said that he considered it his duty to remain in the vicinity of the strait of Juan de Fuca in order to protect Canadian shipping, and that if he steamed in a southerly direction the Canadian ports of Victoria and Vancouver and Canadian shipping in those ports would be without defence. However, his recommendation was not approved and he was ordered to proceed to sea. At that time the Rainbow was without its full complement of officers and ratings. Even with the contingent that was rushed to the Pacific coast from the Niobe, out of an authorized complement of 273 they could muster only 121, of whom forty-four were without previous naval experience. The maximum speed of the Rainbow was sixteen knots; she was without the essential high-explosive ammunition and was proceeding to Vancouver to take on that ammunition when she received this message:
Received from admiralty. Begins. Niimberg and Leipzig reported August 4th off Magdalena bay steering north. Ends. Do your utmost to protect Algerine and Shearwater steering north from San Diego. Remember Nelson and the British navy. All Canada is watching.
Her course was then changed accordingly.
I salute the courage of the officers and men of the Rainbow, who by obedience to that order were sent to what seemed almost certain death. As I have said, the Rainbow had a maximum cruising speed of sixteen knots but could make only fourteen or fifteen knots- on account of leaking steam-joints. She was without high-explosive ammunition and without a full complement of men. Nevertheless, they proceeded to Seattle, where some difficulty was encountered in connection with coaling, and later went down the coast to San Francisco, searching for the Leipzig and the Niimberg. The Leipzig was a light modern cruiser with a maximum speed of twenty-three knots, and with guns which far outranged the Rainbow. The Rainbow missed the Leipzig by three hours in a fog-bank off the coast of San Francisco. That was a courageous act on the part of the men who manned the Rainbow, but little can be said in defence of those who issued the order with its jingoistic flourish: "Remember Nelson and the British navy.-All Canada is watching." That is another blunder in line with those committed by the general staff, with regard to which Sir Robert Borden, as has been revealed in his memoirs, found cause to protest in most vigorous language to the imperial war council. It was a stupid and melodramatic gesture which could easily have ended in disaster. The Rainbow, as I say, missed the Leipzig by only three hours off the coast of San Francisco. It returned to Vancouver, and after it

Foreign Policy-Mr. MacNeil
obtained high-explosive ammunition, for which no fuses were available, it was immediately ordered to put to sea again and engage the Leipzig, and guard trade routes off the coast of San Francisco.
I bring this to the attention of the house because it illustrates three points. The first is that by that order Canada was committed, without the consent of parliament, to an act of participation in external warfare. Of that there can be no doubt. The command to the Rainbow to put to sea to engage the Leipzig and the Niimberg was a belligerent act without any sanction having been given by parliament. It was an order carried out as issued from the admiralty.
The second point is that by reason of the fact that instructions were received under the provisions of the Naval Service Act of Canada, Canadian defence interests were neglected in order to protect two small British sloops which had been dispatched to the Pacific coast to guard seal fisheries.
The third point is that this stupid action illustrates the hopeless muddle in which we again may be placed if we do not clearly place under Canadian command our Canadian armed forces.
This is what actually happened under legislation which is now in force. I submit the unwillingness of the government to amend this legislation in a manner which will make it consonant with our present constitutional status indicates a readiness again to use that legislation if we face a war emergency. I direct the attention of the house to the fact that military writers close to the Department of National Defence have written articles frequently in the last year advocating compulsory military service, and pointing to the fact that in the existing provisions of the Militia Act and Naval Service Act there is ample power to impose military service on all male inhabitants of Canada.
It is said that parliament will decide. I think we should attempt to visualize what may happen. The Minister of Justice the other day went to some pains to explain the difficulties which lie in the way of any attempt to secure the right to neutrality. He did not describe to us what might actually occur if to-morrow Great Britain were involved in war. This has been described clearly in a pamphlet recently issued by a representative and nonpartisan committee. The pamphlet is entitled Canadian Unity in War and Peace. In part it states:
In practice, so long as the present doubt remains, the policy of "parliament will decide" would work out as follows. Let us assume that Great Britain declares war or that war
is declared upon her. For convenience let us call the enemy country State X. Certain consequences at once follow. Canada might immediately be considered the legal enemy of State X on the basis that Canada is at war when Britain is at war. If this did happen, all Canadian trade with State X might, therefore, be stopped, and Canadian or enemy ships clearing for its ports might be refused permission to leave Canadian harbours. "Trading with the enemy" is a crime under Canadian law. All contracts between Canadian corporations and nationals of State X might therefore be automatically dissolved. All this might occur in the interval between Great Britain's entry into the war and the assembling of the Canadian parliament.
In addition, on this view. State X immediately acquires certain legal rights against Canada. Canadian nationals in State X are liable to internment, Canadian property to confiscation, and Canadian ships to seizure. Such events would predetermine the decision of the Canadian parliament by confronting its members with numerous acts of war.
Now let us assume that the Canadian Prime Minister summons the Canadian parliament. This will probably take two weeks. Meanwhile the war progresses and British forces engage in battles on sea and in the air. The press might, on the supposition of automatic involvement, treat Canada as being at war. Canada would be flooded with war propaganda. Extensive preparatory measures would have to be taken by the Canadian Department of National Defence. Canada would be on a war footing and numerous acts of war involving Canadians would almost certainly have occurred before the M.P's reached Ottawa.
Then parliament opens. (The Canadian government may, of course, have announced at the outbreak of war that it intends to take an active part in hostilities, but if it does then it has gone back on the policy of leaving the decision to parliament.) The Prime Minister must then state a policy. If he intends to say, "Gentlemen. I recommend that we declare our neutrality at once," he will be too late. He will find himself entangled by the acts of war and the effects of propaganda. His policy is, therefore, likely to be predetermined for him. and be in effect an acceptance that Canada is at war and a recommendation for assistance to Great Britain. No one believes that he could maintain a position of passive belligerency.
Thus the policy of "parliament will decide" can only mean leaving parliament to decide the amount of the initial grant of money and men for a war already in its third week, not leaving parliament to decide whether or not Canada should enter the war.
And, I would add, by references to the existing Canadian legislation, the governor in council would undoubtedly declare a state of emergency. They would undoubtedly call out the active militia of Canada, and certainly would exercise their power to place Canada in a proper state of defence. But they would also have power, and would probably be under pressure to exercise it, to place the naval and air services in Canada at the disposal of his majesty for service abroad. They would probably be under pressure, and would have auth-
Foreign Policy-Mr. MacNeil

ority to place the militia of Canada available for service abroad-that is, without Canada- for the defence thereof.
They would use exactly the same arguments used by Sir Robert Borden in 1917, when he said, " Clearly a state of emergency exists, and clearly our front line is in France and Belgium." To-day it may be said that if we are thrown into a war, because of British commitments with regard to the Polish frontier, we are in a state of emergency, and that therefore our frontier is coincident with the Polish frontier. That authority exists in these statutes. Furthermore, the power is vested in the governor general to impose compulsory military service on Canada.
I strongly urge, as I did before, that without delay we remove all ambiguity on this vital question, and that action be taken by the government to overhaul and revise these various acts which constitute the articles of war for Canada. .
In conclusion, I would quote the last paragraph of the document to which I referred a moment ago, which was issued by a representative and official committee. I find occasion to agree with the principle expressed therein.
Canadian control over Canadian war policy would merely complete a century of gradual development of democratic control over all aspects of Canada's domestic and foreign affairs. To assert this final democratic right is a natural conclusion to her development into a sovereign nation, linked by feelings of sentiment and a common crown to other British peoples.
