speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, forty-two years ago, speaking at an imperial conference in London, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
England has proved at all times that she can fight her owm battles, but if the day v'ere ever to come when England was in danger, let the bugle sound, let the fires be lit on the hills, and in all parts of the colonies, though we might not he able to do much, whatever we can do shall be done by the colonies to help her.
England did call in 1901, and Canada sent 8,400 men to South Africa. In that number were included the immortal Strathcona Horse, with men and horses, who proved their ability on the field of battle. She sent batteries which were also efficient, and soldiers who were particularly well adapted to that kind
lMr. MacNeil.]
of fighting. But not much in volume of supplies was furnished. But Canada was then in her infancy.
England called again in 1914, and when the bugles sounded and the fires were lit on the hills, forth from her hills and forests, from forge and pit and factory, Canada's man power flocked to the colours-628,000 strong they marched, resourceful, brave, intrepid. They arrived as "bally colonials." They emerged pals and comrades with their English cousins at the peace conference. Canada thus became a nation before that status was confirmed in 1931 at Westminster. Her sons who served in the great war won that honour for her on the field of battle.
Canada's ability to supply not only food, clothing and equipment, but also munitions to the value of over one billion dollars in the great war was a big surprise to England. To-day no one knows Canada's capacity in this regard. It is not a war secret; we just do not know ourselves. If England in her congested areas should suffer from air raiders it is quite likely that Canada alone might supply all her air requirements. In this respect England is fortunate because she has Canada and Australia both embarked already on a great aeroplane construction program, making a type of heavy bombing machine which could be flown across the ocean, if necessary, if the transportation lines were crowded or impaired.
In 1940, co-protectors of liberty for the democracies of north America, surely it is our duty to defend Canada's coast-lines without aid from John Bull or Uncle Sam. If Canada has reached the age of consent-and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) says she has-then she must without a chaperone in this twentieth century rely on her own resources to take the glorious place in history for which we believe she is destined. If we remain true to the blood of our forefathers, French and English, Scotch and Irish, we shall not stand idly by while the United States arms for defence.
As the fourth largest exporting nation and the sixth largest producer in the world, it is within our power to make Canada's comparatively short coast-lines as safe from attack as the rest of America. That is clearly our prime duty. Beyond that, we have vast resources for which there should be a plan of mobilization. So long as we have any unemployed, volunteers might be assisted, perhaps urged, but never coerced, to join the empire forces for service abroad if needed.
There must foe no conscription of men, and there can be no conscription of industry. No army squad under the best sergeant-major,

Foreign Policy-Mr. McAvity
directed by supermen in brass hats, can tune up the wheels of industry like the men who in peace-time make mass production their specialty. If army officers should try to march in and run any Canadian factory, the owners would probably march out. Look to America for light on this question of the mobilization of civilian resources for war. Louis Johnson, assistant secretary for war for the United States, is planning for war-time mobilization of United States industry, and behind him the best brains in that country are planning mobilization of capital and labour and of all supplies, so that the entire resources of the nation may be lined up if an emergency arises. The democracies to-day should adopt the boy scout motto-" Be prepared." Franklin D. Roosevelt had the United States navy prepared and ready in 1917. I called, shortly after the United States had entered the war, at the ordnance department of the United States navy, and I was told by the admiral in charge of ordnance that there was no rush in that department, no congestion, no confusion. During his period of office as under-secretary of the navy, Franklin D. Roosevelt sent word to the best manufacturers in the United States, and had them come in and prepare contracts which were all complete except for signature, so that the moment war was declared, telegrams confirmed the contracts and everything was ready in the navy ordnance department. But it was not so in the army.
It did not cost much to put that preparedness plan into effect. National defence does cost and is costing all nations an appalling sum to-day. But modern war, if it comes, will need more than can be provided by any department of national defence alone. The whole resources of the nation must be planned and organized. The contest in the final analysis will be between one set of manufacturing resources and another. England is fortunate in having her scattered democracies comparatively safely situated, rich in resources, with Australia and Canada at least having a good supply of skilled workmen available.
I want to quote from the Congressional Digest what Bernard M. Baruch said before the senate committee on military affairs:
We have learned that modern war is not the impact of a few men. The whole nation, with its every resource, must be thrown against the enemy. The welfare of the civilian population must be systematically provided for as well as that of the soldiers. . . .
A modern war effort, with responsibilities and safeguards equally distributed, comprises these three things:
1.	Raising and training the fighting manpower.
2.	Equipment and supplying of the same with fighting materials and with transportation, with payment as you go to the fullest extent possible.
3.	Protection of the civilian population against rising living costs due to inflation by holding down prices for materials and services in connection with number 2.
The raising and training of the fighting man power is clearly a technical question to be left to the technical officers of the army, navy and air force. The equipment and supplying of the same with fighting materials is clearly a civilian affair to be handled by civilians.
As to the third item, the protection of the civilian population against rising living costs, during the last war the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett acted as chairman, without pay, of the national service council, but in New Brunswick Captain L. P. Tilley acted as director for that province at $250 a month. I submit that we need something more substantial if we are faced with another like emergency.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) made some observations about profits in the manufacture of munitions. In that connection I should like to quote again from Mr. Baruch. Speaking in 1937-and some progress has been made since that time -Mr. Baruch said:
May I add just one more warning note? A phrase much heard is "take the profit out of war." I, myself, have used that phrase so often that sometimes I think I invented it. Yet one must realize that it expresses an ideal rather than an actual goal. Taxes of all kinds should be increased. Profits should be only what are necessary to get what we need for the army and civilians. Profits can be kept down well below peace-time levels, but they cannot be abolished. Let no one mislead you on that score. To attempt to abolish all profit would mean another attempt to embark upon a sea of economic experiment that has never been successfully navigated. Our whole industrial and economic machine is built and geared to run on profit and reward for personal initiative. There is no proof that it will run on psychology and much that it will not. Certainly, when the enemy is at our gates is not the hour to try to find out.
Certainly when the enemy is at our gates is not the hour to try to find out.
Mention was made of the enormous profits made by manufacturers in the last war. I want to say a word in that regard so far as it concerns the manufacture of shells. Prices were fixed, and they were fixed low. Any manufacturer who took an order for shells ran many risks. There was the risk of not getting machinery, the risk of not getting labour; labour prices rose; everything had to come by express; there was risk in the matter of inspection. If a manufacturer were
Foreign Policy-Mr. McAvity

fortunate in making any profit under these conditions, the Minister of Finance had the war tax to take it away from him. Therefore it was a case of "heads I win, tails you lose." If the manufacturer lost money nobody made it up to him, and if he made any profit it was taxed away from him.
There has been considerable talk both in England and in the United States, and I think the feeling is strong here, that the profits should be reduced to a minimum. The last word I have read on that is from Winston Churchill, who suggests that no one should come out of a war richer than he went in. He said:
This could be achieved by assessing the value of undertakings at the outbreak of war on the basis of the information available to the revenue department and by insisting that nobody should be better off at the end of the war than at the beginning. Hardships would arise in the case of businesses just about to expand but no man would have cause for complaint if he found himself at the end of the war as well off as he was at the beginning.
I want to say a few words about our local situation, at the port of Saint John.
Located on our eastern coast-line, Saint John is vulnerable to attack. Requests were made last week by our worthy mayor, Mr. D. L. MacLaren, and Squadron Leader Wendell W. Rogers for adequate and modern defences. These we hope and believe will be constructed without delay by order of the Minister of National Defence, (Mr. Mackenzie). If Great Britain is at war and Canada is supplying materials for war, who can doubt that enemy raiders will attempt continuously to cut off communication between Canada and the motherland, at the port of Saint John, with its docks, elevators, railway terminals, the bridge across the river, oil tanks, hospitals and general facilities. The Saint John dry dock is one of the largest in the world. I cannot see how the loyalist city of Saint John could ever be neutral if England were at war. Everyone knows how busy both Halifax and Saint John were during the last war. Earlier in the session I drew the attention of this house to the need for adequate storage warehouses, and a concise plan to be worked out in conjunction with the Department of National Defence for war-time use and protection of Atlantic ports. I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) to order that a plan be prepared for both Atlantic ports and direct railroad connection to both ports as an integral and essential part of Canada's scheme for defence. It will not cost much to prepare the plans, and it is easier to make them before an emergency arises.

I have just one last word. A small clipping I took from the New York Times quotes an item by Alexander Hamilton, written one hundred and fifty years ago. It is this:
A cloud has been for some time hanging over the European world. If it should break forth into a storm, who can ensure that in its progress a part of its fury would not be spent upon us?
The rights of neutrality will only be respected when they are defended by an adequate power. A nation, despicable by its weakness, forfeits even the privilege of being neutral.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem of our external relations has always been very important, but the events of the last two years and1 of recent days have made it foremost.
Since about two years, rumours of war in Europe have been more or less current. Great Britain, by reason of its economic interests, cannot remain indifferent to developments which endanger her world markets; the possibility of her becoming involved in armed conflict as a result has given rise to the question of Canadian participation in empire wars.
The question is not a new one, but since the Statute of Westminster it has taken a new aspect, and it is important to solve it according to the spirit of this new charter.
It is at present a cause of uneasiness in this country, and if we do not want this uneasiness to continue, with regrettable consequences, it is essential that we should state our position in clear and unmistakable terms.
It is undeniable that the Canadian people are far from being unanimous on the attitude to take in the event of a war involving England. Whence comes the difference of opinion? It must be admitted that too many people do not want to think and act as true Canadians.
Reason, and not sentiment, should dictate the approach to the question, especially in a country peopled by subjects of diverse origins. For my part, it is as a Canadian purely and simply, and in the sole light of Canadian interests, that I intend to discuss it.
What should be our attitude in the event of a foreign war involving England? Our attitude should be dictated by our interest and by our determination to maintain peace at home and peace with other countries. Such is the attitude taken by the Prime Minister in the remarkable speech, stamped with Cana-dianism, which he delivered on the 24th of May last, at a time when the European situation was very tense:
In times of world disturbance, the policies of no two countries can be alike, provided they are rooted in their own interests or the ideals in which their interests are sublimated, and

Foreign Policy-Mr. Raymond
are not merely echoes of the policies of other our position in clear and unmistakeable terms, countries.
This is how the Prime Minister defined our external policy:
Our foreign and external policy is a policy of peace and friendliness, a policy of trying to look after our own interests. ... It is a policy which takes account of . . . our geographical situation, the limited numbers and the racial composition of our people, our stage in economic development, our own internal preoccupations and necessities-in short, a policy based on the Canadian situation.
And further:
We have neither the power nor the will to attack aiiy other land for our own ends. Nor are we inclined to organize or join in crusades in other continents. .	.	. We have neither
the power nor the knowledge to settle the destinies of countries thousands of miles away. We are no more likely of our own motion to intervene in Europe than Sweden or Bulgaria or Switzerland is to intervene in America.
All those who rejoice in the fact that Canada has become a free and sovereign nation and absolute mistress of her own policy, have greeted with satisfaction these clear and unequivocal statements.
According to the Prime Minister, our external policy was on May 24 last a policy of peace and friendliness based on our own interests and admitting of no probability of intervention in Europe. This attitude is in full accordance with the rule followed by all free peoples.
A few months later, on December 12th last, the Prime Minister of England made the following reply in the British House of Commons:
No treaty or agreement with France places us under any specific obligation to grant any military assistance to that country in the event of her being attacked by Italy.
And the following day, at the Foreign Press dinner, he stated in unmistakable terms England's position in regard to France:
Our relations with France go far beyond purely legal obligations; they are based on identity of interests.
It must not be forgotten, indeed, that national interests are often a better guarantee than treaties or ephemeral alliances.
To complete this argument, I shall quote the opinion of a prominent French author, Lucien Romier, who wrote as follows:
The state, in its relations with other states is the very expression of national egoism, and statesmen cannot rid themselves of this egoism without betraying their mandate.
As to the question of participation in an armed conflict involving the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister of Canada said in the same speech of May 24th last:
Parliament will decide upon our course.
And he quoted a previous statement made at Geneva in September 1936:
The Canadian parliament reserves to itself the right to declare, in the light of the circumstances existing at the time, to what extent, if at all, Canada will participate in conflicts in which other members of the commonwealth may be engaged.
And further:
The simple fact of being part of the British Empire does not necessarily involve us in a war in which other parts of the British Empire may be engaged.
There has apparently been a change since then. What has happened? Would it be due to the events of September last, which brought Europe within an ace of war?
However it may be, on January 16th last, the Prime Minister, speaking in the house, resurrected an old formula of colonial times which he adopted as his own:
When England is at war, we are at war and subject to attack.
That, to my mind, is a return to colonial days. What has become of the end so obstinately and successfully pursued since 1921 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) ?
On March 20th, in a carefully prepared statement, the Prime Minister anticipated the decision of Parliament in the event of there being a prospect of an aggressor bombing London from the air. And Friday last the Minister of Justice specified that the decision would be one of intervention.
Such a policy, in my opinion, implies Canada's participation in a European war; it is an invitation to aggression and a menace to national unity.	_
In the face of this situation, I wish to state to the house my views, which are those of the very great majority of the people I represent, as expressed in numerous resolutions. In this connection, I may point out that my constituency of Beauhamois-Laprairie comprises the county of Laprairie, formerly represented by Dominique Monet, who in 1899 opposed the sending of Canadian contingents to South Africa, and later on by Roch Lanctot, who was a strong opponent of military appropriations.
Why should we join in an extra-territorial war involving Great Britain? We have no legal obligation. We are free. The Prime Minister pointed this out on several occasions, notably in a speech which he delivered on July 19th, 1937, on his return from an imperial conference:
The delegates to the conference unanimously agreed on the full liberty of action of each government in the domain of foreign policy, of defence and in other matters. They also laid equal emphasis on the fact that their parliaments remained supreme in those fields.
Foreign Policy-Mr. Raymond

The then Prime Minister of England, Mr. Baldwin, had already recognized that:
The members of the British commonwealth of nations were absolutely free to decide for themselves upon their defence policy. (British House of Commons, February 22, 1937.)
On August 25, 1938, at Toronto, Lord Stanley, then Secretary for Dominion Affairs, stated:
Is Canada at war when Great Britain is at war? Certainly not. Canada makes her own decisions. She is a sovereign nation and decides for herself.
On December 5 last, in the British House of Commons, Mr. Chamberlain admitted that:
Canada has the right to decide for herself whether she should come to ;he assistance of Great Britain in case of attack.
Furthermore, the statute of Westminster gives Canada the right to avoid interfering in a war in which England takes part. We have no obligation-let us act accordingly.
Would we take part in an armed conflict in Europe, in Africa or in Asia, in order to serve our interest or the interest of the British empire?
It is agreed that every country must base and effectively bases its actions on its own interest. Well, I wonder what interest we would have to fight three or four thousand miles away from our frontiers. Surely it would not ibe to defend our territory; it is easier to protect ourselves at home rather than three to four thousand miles from our borders.
Would we go to war in order to satisfy a lust for conquest?
We have no territorial ambition. We have proved it during the war of 1914. We went to that war and came back from it. But that experience has cost us, so far, approximately 5 billions of dollars and it will cost us 160 millions per year for an indefinite period; we have had 60,000 killed, a great number of wounded, etc. Among the victorious countries, only Canada received nothing, while Great Britain, for whose sake we fought, benefited from the victory by an increase of the empire in the form of colonial mandates, the possibility of increasing the international trade which is its very life, and by the destruction of the German fleet.
Would we go to war in order to protect our trade?
First of all, our oceanic trade is done by English or foreign boats which those countries have an interest to protect in order to insure their own food supplies. Moreover, according to an article published by Professor Scott in Foreign Affairs of January, 1939, the cost of a war would far exceed the amount of our exports.
fMr. Raymond.1
Would we go to war in order to save
democracy and ensure peace?
That was the slogan in 1914. What a success it was! We were to save democracy and civilization, and we in reality prepared the advent of dictatorships. We were to ensure universal peace, and never before have rumours of war been more persistent. And such were the achievements of the victors of the great European war to which we participated, because every victorious nation, with the exception of Canada, sought to obtain the greatest benefits from victory. *
Would we go to war in order to protect our territory and our lives?
We are protected by our geographical situation and by our neighbours: the Arctic ocean on the north, the Atlantic on the east, the Pacific on the west and the United States on the south.
We are protected by the statements of the President of the United States who has promised to defend this country against anj external attack.
We are protected by the declaration of Lima on the solidarity of American nations, which entails the defence of the territory of America against any interference from a foreign power.
Finally, we are protected by our friendly relations with all countries.
While on the subject of the Lima Conference, let me express the regret, sir, that Canada was not represented there, especially when our interests were at stake and when a vacant seat is reserved for Canada in the Pan-American Union Hall in Washington.
The prime minister told us that Canada could not be invited as it is not a member of the Pan-American Union. But is not that vacant seat an invitation in itself, or at least the first step in our direction? Canada could or should have taken the second step.
Is it not in the interest of our country, which is an American country, to take part in Pan-American conferences, as it is in the interest of other countries of America?
We take part in European conferences; we are represented at the League of Nations, and all that costs much money. In certain quarters, we are even asked to participate in a European war, under colour of defending peace and democracy, against totalitarian states, or under pretence of defending Canada. But when, on this continent, all American countries gather together in order to seek means of defending democracy and peace against totalitarian states, of defending American territory, Canada, which is an American country, keeps aloof.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Raymond
I seriously wonder if it was for fear of injuring the interests of the British empire? And we have cause to ask ourselves if our foreign policy is not dictated by London; if we really are as free as we are told, free to look after our interests first, or if we are in the tow of England.
As a nation, we have the right to shape our foreign policy which must be based on our needs, independently of the needs of other countries. We must look to our own interests, which lie on the American continent.
Would we go to war in order to play in Europe the part of a policeman, and to bring to reason nations which are infinitely more powerful than we are, and for what purpose, in some cases? When it is remembered that Europe, and ourselves perhaps, were on the verge of war, last September, to prevent a minority of 31 million Sudeten Germans to free themselves from a rule of mean intolerance and almost oppression, according to the expressions used in the report of Lord Runciman, who was especially sent by England in order to investigate and who recognized the justice of their grievances. It was the result of the treaty of Versailles, of which Mr. Chamberlain said, recently:
If, twenty years ago, the frontiers had been
better drawn, there would not have been a Czechoslovakian crisis.
Inasmuch as we have no interest in taking part in such external conflicts, why should we go to war? To defend the interests of others while ruining ourselves? No true Canadian has the right to do such a thing.
Knowing that wars are brought about by conflicting interests, to what dangers of war are we not exposed?
Let us recall some of the events of recent times.
A year ago, the three main dangers of war came from the far east, Spain and central Europe.
What were the causes of discord between the countries involved? They were matters of commercial or economic interests, and questions of prestige.
Let us take the case of Czechoslovakia, which threatened, two or three times, to set are to Europe and even to this country.
What was the situation in that artificial state, created after the war to hem in Germany and to serve the interests of France -a state that nothing could make homogeneous and which was destined to be a permanent cause of trouble?
The Czech government persisted in refusing all concessions to the Sudeten people, a minority of German origin which asked for its share of public offices or in the govem-71492-161$
ment of the country; claims whose justice was recognized by Lord Runciman, the representative of England.
What was the attitude of London in that case, and what was the attitude of Ottawa?
Was it an ideological conflict? Ideological conflicts are a joke, they do not exist.
Was it a political or an economical conflict? After all, we must know what is at stake, what we would be fighting for.
Listen to what Mr. Chamberlain said, on September 27, in a radio broa,dcast:
How horrible, fantastic, incredible, that we should be digging trenches here and fitting gas masks, on account of a conflict in a far-away country, between people, of whom we know nothing.	_
However much one may sympathize with a small nation confronted by a big and powerful nation, we cannot in all circumstances undertake to involve the whole British empire in a war simply on that account. If we have to fight, it must be on larger issues than that.
The following day, September 28, the eve of the Munich conference, Mr. Chamberlain, speaking in the House of Commons, indicated the alternative courses of action open to him in the deadlock where he found himself.
We could have threatened to go to war with Germany if she attacked Czechoslovakia, he said, but we had no treaty liabilities to Czechoslovakia.
Indeed, this country, he said further, would not have followed us if we had tried to lead it into war to prevent a minority from obtaining autonomy. .
That last sentence indicates what the stakes would have been in such a war.
And Sir John Simon, speaking in the House of Commons on the 19th December last, said:
The Agreement of Munich was transferring to the Reich an area which ought not to have been included in Czechoslovakia. What we did was to correct one of the mistakes of the Peace Treaty.
In truth, what interest had we in that dispute, when the Prime Minister of England himself agreed that it was a matter of participating in a war, waged in a remote country, between people we knew nothing about, in order to prevent a minority from securing its autonomy, and when the chancellor of the exchequer, Sir John Simon, admitted that the transfer of that area to the Reich was merely correcting a mistake of the peace treaty.
However, the cabinet held emergency meetings and the Prime Minister stated that he was prepared to summon parliament, so that effective and concerted action might be taken.
Here is the statement which the Prime Minister gave to the press on the 28th September:	[DOT]
The government is making preparations for any contingency and for the immediate sum-

Foreign Policy-Mr. Raymond,
moning of parliament if the efforts being made to preserve the peace fail. For our country, to keep united is all-important. To this end, in whatever we say or do, we must seek to avoid creating controversies which might seriously impair effective and concerted action when parliament meets.
Let us compare the attitude of M. Spaak, prime minister of Belgium, a truly free country, but quite open to attack in Europe; on the 18th September, he said that:
There was no need to assemble parliament or to make any special declaration, as the government would continue to follow their settled policy of independence.
The Prime Minister often tells us "we have no commitment." Then what is the reason of the present attitude?
We had no commitment to participate in a war for the defence of Czechoslovakia. Canada was not threatened, neither was England, but, nevertheless, because England was contemplating military action the Prime Minister appeared ready to commit Canada to participation in an external war in which we were not concerned.
If, on that occasion, England contemplated military action, it was not because she had a treaty with Czechoslovakia-she had none. It was not because she had a moral cause to defend-such was not the case. It was merely because France was bound by virtue of a treaty with Czechoslovakia to fight in defence of the latter and because England, in order to maintain the European balance, an old policy she has ever pursued on account of her trade interests in all parts of the world, did not want to see France overwhelmed by Germany, whose rearmament she had nevertheless encouraged ever since the treaty of Versailles so that the seesaw game between France and Germany would still continue.
She has always resorted to that seesaw game, as for instance in Palestine between Jews and Arabs, and in India between Hindoos and Moslems. Nowadays, political and economic ambitions outweigh all other ideals.
This explains why England took a different attitude towards nationalist Spain, from the day General Franco took Bilbao and seized iron mines in the vicinity of that city.
Let us not forget that war waged for ideological motives is a hoax of which we are the victims.
Let us consider that during the war between China and Japan, while the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo axis was in process of formation, and Germany was allied to Japan, German officers were training the Chinese to fight the. Japanese and were directing Chinese resistance; Chinese flyers were being instructed by Italian airmen.
IMr. Raymond.]
Let us consider that while Italian and German soldiers were fighting in the ranks of Franco's army in Spain, Germany was shipping supplies to the Reds. She was fighting for Burgos but was supplying materials to Barcelona.
At the time when American ships were being bombed and sunk, the United States was selling petroleum to Japan.
While Mussolini was breaking off negotiations with France, under the pretext that she had become too much sovietized, he had in Moscow an ambassador who was entering into trade agreements with the Soviets.
During the war in Ethiopia, important purchases of coal were made in France for shipment to Eritrea via Djibouti; such purchases were even guaranteed by the French government.
While England was showing uneasiness about the growing power of Germany, she was not neglecting her trade with the latter; only last year, she sold her textiles for a value of thirty million dollars.
As a keen observer has said: "Each one is trying to fool the others. And they would have us fight for Truth."
At the present time, Germany is claiming her former colonies and Italy is demanding certain concessions in Suez, Djibouti and Tunisia. What is involved in such cases? As ever before, it is a matter of conflicting interests.
The British Admiralty Council consider that any important change in the statu quo of the port of Djibouti would be contrary to British interests, particularly as regards the British possessions of Aden.
In the Mediterranean area, it is important that French Tunisia should jointly protect the route to India.
The greater interests of England's empire lie in Asia and in the lines of communication leading thereto. She has to protect them.
Palestine is for England the land and air route to India. It is also a base for the defence of the Suez canal; it is the outlet for the petroleum from Mossul.
On the 6th February last, Mr. Chamberlain stated in the House of Commons that:
any threat to the vital interests of France, from whatever quarter it might come, would entail England's immediate cooperation.
For what purpose would Canada risk being ruined in a war merely to maintain for England and France, now working in cooperation, their colonial empires, which are the two greatest in the world? We have no colonies to give back.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Raymond
After all, if the international situation is tense, Canada is in no way to blame. And why should we be governed by the principle whereby if England is at war Canada is at war?
Canada had absolutely nothing to do with the situation brought about by Mr. Benes, who failed or refused to carry out the pledges given to the minorities of his country. Canada was not, either, a party to the treaty signed by France and Czechoslovakia with the object of guaranteeing the security of the latter.
It was no fault of Canada's if France was confronted with internal difficulties which so weakened her that she had to seek the help of England, for the protection of the French colonial empire.
It was no fault of Canada's if France blundered into creating ill feelings which may endanger European peace.
It was no fault of Canada's if the sympathies of the Popular Front government stirred up the hostility of Franco, of Italy and of Germany; if France stubbornly refused to appoint an ambassador to Rome and a representative to Burgos.
Who was responsible for the formation of the Rome-Berlin axis after the Stresa conference? England, through her insistence upon the imposition of economic sanctions during the Italo-Ethiopian conflict. Italy, who must care for 4 or 5 million workmen although practically deprived of raw materials, who must every day import bread, meat, textiles, partly manufactured goods, coal, and petroleum, whose sources of supply are unstable, was threatened with famine and ruin and therefore compelled to join Germany.-and we are now suffering the consequences thereof.
Is it Canada's fault if Germany has become strong and powerful through violation of every treaty?
Was it not Great Britain who, in order to maintain the traditional balance of power which is at the base of her world supremacy, stood by without protest as Germany rearmed by means of the money which should have been paid to France? (According to a well-informed political writer, Andre Tardieu, Germany is supposed to have paid France only 6 per cent of the amount stipulated in the treaties, and 2 per cent of what the war cost France.) Who permitted the reestablishment of compulsory military service in March, 1935, and the military occupation of the Rhineland district in March, 1936? Who agreed to the Anglo-German Naval Accord in 1935?
For the last twenty years, Great Britain has been the best advocate of German recovery. Why should we be called upon to help pay the cost of these mistakes?
It is no fault of Canada's that England has great investments in Roumanian oil fields and is now contemplating pledging herself to guarantee the latter's safety.
It is no fault of Canada's that England possesses the greatest colonial empire in the world and is forced to maintain a mighty military machine in order to ensure her freedom of communications.
It is no fault of Canada's that France possesses the second greatest colonial empire in the world, which England, because of their identity of interests, has pledged herself to defend against any attack.
It is no fault of Canada's that London and Paris have just guaranteed the independence of Poland,
It is not our fault that England and France possess and have to safeguard immense resources everywhere, and very often next door to ambitious or needy countries.
It is no fault of ours, yet we must not forget to weigh the consequences of our participation in any empire wars in accordance with the statement: "When England is at war, Canada is at war."
This implies that we are tacitly bound to share in the defence of the British colonial empire, of the French colonial empire, of Poland, of Roumania, etc., etc.; that we are continually in danger of being drawn into a conflict which would inevitably spell our downfall.
Everyone is agreed that the next war will produce nothing but ruins and that even for the belligerents who shall achieve military success, the victory will be an empty one.
There appeared in the Ottawa Journal the day after Munich the following statement:
War for Canada, war such as we participated in the last time, would have meant bankruptcy.
Therefore, do I say that Canada must not be involved in a war wherein she is neither attacked nor threatened; we have not the right to sacrifice our entire youth and to court ruin merely to safeguard the economic and commercial advantages or supremacy of any European country, whether French or British.
Another consequence thereof, and not the least disastrous, would be disunion among our people.
It is the bounden duty of those who are charged with high responsibilities to see that such a tragedy is averted.
The advocates of participation and those who oppose it are already forming sides and growing restless.
As a matter of fact, a policy which favours participation in a war which is no direct or immediate concern of ours cannot be looked upon surely as a contribution to national unity,
Foreign Policy-Mr. Raymond

and for my part I could never endorse a policy which would set at odds with one another the various component bodies of the nation.
Canada, a sovereign country, occupies a unique position in America'. We have no possessions elsewhere, no colonies, no protectorates nor mandates; our interests are centered in America. And Canadian unity will never be threatened as long as we restrict ourselves to the safeguarding of those interests, and require the Canadian people to provide foi the defence of their own country, but of no other.
I realize that there are, and quite naturally, strong bonds of sympathy uniting Canadians of English origin to England, and that Canadians of French origin feel the same way towards France, but I also know that there are a great many Canadians whose sympathies are directed elsewhere. And I believe that we, in autonomous Canada, have one great obligation towards one another, which is that of acting in the best interests of the country of our choice.
Let us never forget Lord Tweedsmuir's statement;
The first duty of a Canadian is to Canada.
Let us therefore adopt a policy tending to ensure peace, especially internal peace which is even more vital than the other. The dismemberment of Czechoslovakia should be a salutary lesson in this regard.
Let us not endanger the internal peace of Canada by deciding to participate in any war for the defence of foreign interests.
The Canadians of French origin are Canadians first; they are strongly bound to Canada, their mother country, and their only desire is to strive for her development in harmony and peace, with the protection of two mighty oceans and of the great American nation. They hate war but do not fear it when it is a matter of defending their own soil, as history will bear witness. Let us not force them to defend foreign lands and thereby invite their own ruin.
Wars that are waged to set aright the wrong done to another, often give rise to greater misfortune at home. If 1917 has been forgiven, it has not been forgotten.
We must consider as very good friends the other members of the commonwealth, but friendship should not prevail over selfpreservation. Moreover, what right has one to ask his friend to agree to a sacrifice which is far beyond his means?
Any external policy which would require from the Canadian people more than that which any patriot or any citizen who loves his

country and desires to protect it would be glad to do, would risk shattering for evermore our national unity.
Every Canadian citizen has the military obligation of defending the soil of his motherland, and those of the province of Quebec have never shirked that duty, nor shall they ever do so, but no one is entitled to ask them to go and shed their blood in Europe, or in Africa, or in Asia for the greater glory or power of any other country, even if that country should be England or France.
And if ever a majority of the people of this country should desire to compel an important minority thereof to take up arms in defence of a foreign land, whichever it may be, that would be the end of confederation.
Following the example set by the Premier of France, M. Daladier, who said that Munich had been an act of reason, let us adopt a policy based not on emotions but on reason, and as the right hon. the Minister of Justice stated in a speech he gave in Quebec, last December 12;
Instead of waging war in a foreign land, we shall remain at home and defend Canada whom we love.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of reluctance that I participate in this debate, but it seems to be in order that we should all have something to say about this extremely important matter. In commencing my remarks I wish to make it clear that I believe sincerely in the British empire, the British commonwealth of nations. I believe in its past and its present; I believe that it yet has before it a great and splendid future, not great necessarily in the sense that we shall go forth to conquer but rather that we as a people shall live worthy lives, meriting the respect and honour of the world, so managing ourselves that we can be looked up to and that we ourselves may be happy.
No man at this time is in a position to foresee what will come. We are in perhaps the most uncertain age the world has ever known. We must look forward with great faith, confident, however, that there is before us a great future and that the world does not need to be in a condition in which its peace is endangered and its happiness insecure.
I believe that we as an empire and as a commonwealth, sir, can easily assume the role of leading the world into a better time, not by aggression but by living as a people ought to live. Furthermore I realize vividly that the British governments to-day might be, and probably are, motivated by forces over which the British peoples cannot now exercise

Foreign Policy-Mr. Blackmore
control. These forces govern the instruments of propaganda. These forces are not concerned primarily with the welfare of the British people or of the British commonwealth of nations. I wish furthermore to lay down this principle that our task is, in my opinion, so to manage Canada's policy that we may best be enabled to help save the British peoples, first from external and visible enemies and, second, from perhaps equally dangerous internal and invisible enemies. Further, I Ihink we all implicitly believe in democracy. These four statements having been made, to commence with, if we can all agree upon them we can proceed to examine the possible principles upon which we can govern our behaviour and lay down our foreign policy.
As I see it, there are five main questions which are vividly and perhaps painfully before the people of Canada to-day. They are questions to which everyone wants the answers, if I may judge by what has been said in the debate, and by what I have heard outside. The first question is: Shall Canadians fight? The second is: Can Canada be neutral while Great Britain fights? The third is: Tf Canada fights, where will she fight? The fourth: How shall we prepare to fight; and the fifth: Can we do anything to try to avoid fighting, by such means as removing the causes of war, or organizing a form of collective security?
It is well that before we go farther we lay down the principle that the opinion of the people of Canada changes from week to week, and, in these hectic times, almost from hour to hour. I saw the results of a questionnaire which had been placed before the students of many Canadian universities. The report of the results was designed to show the change which in one year had come over the students in those universities. Whereas a year ago a majority of them were against fighting, to-day the majority were in favour of fighting.
A great change has come over the Canadian people in the present year. Who is to say that an equally great change may not come over our people in the next three months or three weeks? It seems to me that for a government or parliament to say definitely just what it will do in a month from now is certainly a reckless procedure. It seems to me the function of a democratic government is to hold itself free from entanglements so that at all times it can do the thing which the people it governs desire it shall do. My whole attitude towards this question is based on that assumption. The government of a democratic people is placed in office to do what the people desire it to do. It should take such measures as may be
practicable to keep the people informed concerning the truth regarding the drama being enacted before them internationally; then the people themselves must decide.
I have all faith in the people of Canada. Give them the truth, and they will form correct conclusions. During the last few days while we have been having this debate I have been interested to note, while walking along the streets, the conversation of people whom I have passed. One will hear little groups of men discussing the great problems we discuss in the house, and apparently they bring to their discussions just as much keenness, intelligence and ability as we exercise in the house. Public opinion of Canada is being formed from hour to hour. All the people need is the truth to work upon, and they will find what is right and will demand that we do what is right.
Now to come to the five questions respecting which Canadians want answers. First, shall Canada fight? The feeling, as I gather it, is developing rapidly throughout the country that Canada will fight. She will fight for three things, those three things laid down by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson), in his excellent talk. She will fight for civilization; she will fight for liberty, and she will fight for the integrity of Canada's soil. Perhaps there would be other things, but at least at this stage of our thinking I believe those three may be pretty well taken for granted.
Can Canada be neutral? On this question there has been a great deal of learned and able discussion in the house. A number of people feel that legally Canada can remain neutral, and a number of people quite as earnestly urge that she cannot. Perhaps if all the facts were in evidence it would form a delicate question for the decision of the highest court in the land. I fancy, however, that when the time comes, we shall not trouble ourselves very much about legal technicalities. If the people of Canada choose to fight, they will fight. If they choose not to fight, they will not fight. But -we might talk about the matter academically to some extent, in this way: What would be the democratic way of dealing with the question? Led by the excellent speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in the house we have pretty well laid down the principle that we will not stand for conscription in Canada. Why do we say that? Because we say it is the citizen's right to determine what he shall do. No one has the right to say that some other person shall go to offer his life unless that person chooses to do so. That is democracy.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Blackmore
Well, now, would it not be a sound principle to lay down that if iwe allow the individual citizen the right to determine whether or not he shall fight we should certainly allow the individual state to have the equal right to determine whether or not it will fight. If we follow that line of reasoning, then it does look as though we should lay down the principle in Canada, sooner or later, legally- whether up to the present time we have laid it down legally and constitutionally-that this country through its parliament and government must at all times have the complete right to determine whether or not it will fight. I would say that the hon. member for Selkirk was on perfectly safe ground. I rather fancy that before very long we should lay down this principle, that Canada has the right, legal, constitutional and in every other way, to remain neutral in another war if she chooses to do so. Whether or not Canada will exercise that right is another matter entirely. If I can establish for my neighbour's boy that he has the right to stay out of the army if he chooses to do so, I am not deciding that he will stay out of the army; I am merely establishing his right to do so. I think in time we shall all recognize that it is Canada's right to stay out of any war whatsoever. The thing which finally will determine my iboy and my neighbour's boy to join the army will be this, that they will realize that their country's welfare is at stake, and that unless they go and play their part they cannot expect their neighbours to go and play their part, and consequently all will suffer.
The same sort of reasoning should determine Canada, in case she and her neighbour nations are in danger of losing their collective security, that she must com-e in and help. She will realize that she has a responsibility, and she will accept it. She does not need to be bound by any legal or constitutional commitment whatsoever. The people themselves must decide whether they will fight, when they will fight, where they will fight, and to what extent they will fight, both individually and collectively as a nation. I think the Canadian people generally are pretty well agreed on that principle. They do not wish to express it in a loud, aggressive way, so as to make it appear that they are disloyal, but deep down in their hearts they feel it.
Now where shall Canada fight? There exists a great deal of uncertainty and perturbation throughout Canada concerning this question. A good many are afraid that they might be committed to go and fight in Poland, for example; many were afraid they might be called on to go and fight in Czechoslovakia, and they were not quite sure whether they

wanted to fight in Czechoslovakia. There was a question at issue there. Where shall Canada fight? I would hesitate to lay down any principle, for the simple reason that the opinions of the Canadian people will perhaps be different three weeks from now from what they are to-day, but I might raise three or four questions which would guide us all in forming an opinion.

Very true. Suppose I am a Canadian who does not want to go overseas and fight in a foreign battle line. Would I be willing to fight in Nova Scotia, to protect Nova Scotia? I think nearly everyone will say, "Yes, of course." Now would I go and fight, in Newfoundland? I think it would be difficult for any Canadian to say that he would not go and defend Newfoundland, right at our gates.
Here is another question. Would I enlist upon a warship and go out into the waters to meet an enemy ship which was coming to attack my country? It would mean I was leaving my native shore of Canada. Would I be an air pilot and go out over the water and fight?
