subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Beyond the three-mile limit?
Mr. BLACKMO*RE:	Yes, beyond the
three-mile limit. I think the answer in nearly every case would be yes. Having once gone as far as that, where are you going to stop? Would you go half way across the Atlantic to meet the foe? All these are questions we have to ask ourselves in order to think realistically on this subject, and I believe the Canadian people	are thinking	their waythrough	in quite	an admirable	manner.	I
believe they will arrive at a conclusion which will enable them to stand behind their government when the time comes, if it comes, although of course we all pray it will not.
The next question is: How shall we prepare to fight? Concerning that there is much heailt-searching by a great many earnest people. Shall we put conscription into force in case we get in grave danger? The first question	we shall	have to ask ourselves	inthinking	our way	through that	problem	is
this: Is conscription democratic? The answer has to be no; it is not democratic; there is no question about that. That fact argues strongly against it. I believe I would be prepared to lay down unalterably and irrevocably the principle that there shall be no conscription whatsoever. The voluntary system has been in use in our empire for generations, and has

Foreign Policy-Mr. Blackmore
not failed us yet. I see no reason for doubting the quality of the youth of this generation any more than we did the youth of past generations. I believe the voluntary system will carry us through every war however great, that we need to be carried through; when the British people have so far decayed that they need conscription to force them into battle, then perhaps the British race will be no longer worthy of being saved and we should be prepared to give up the British flag and all the values we hold so dear.
There are several fundamental reasons why conscription is not sound and why the voluntary system is better. We have developed through the centuries a reputation which was represented in a fine poem that came out of Canada through the last war. The poem closes with the ringing line:
But beware of a peace-loving people
When they sweep from their forests and farms.
When men rise and go to fight of their own accord they are terrible men, and they fight in a way which appals their enemy. I think our men are still of the British breed, still carry British blood in their veins. They are fired with British traditions and, given half a chance, will prove themselves worthy of their fathers, not only in a war which might be immediately confronting us, but in any war, near or remote. So again I would say, let us have no conscription under any circumstances.
There is another reason why conscription is not good. So long as a government knows that it, must depend on the goodwill of the people for voluntary service, that serves as a check upon the government. If war comes and profiteering is permitted like what took place in the last war, and if people are afraid of poverty after the war, there will not be such a rush to volunteer. There are nasty rumours abroad, which I have heard ever since the war, that there was, in a good many instances, mistreatment of men who went overseas. I would say that if that occurred in another war there would be a distinct falling off in enlistment, and there should be strong pressure on the men who were mistreating soldiers and mismanaging the war. That is a something which needs to be taken care of. We need a check on such possible abuses, for men sometimes do forget to be human, even in war, and they also forget to be reasonable.
But people will say, what will you do if you cannot get volunteers? The first thing is to find out why you cannot get volunteers and remove the causes. The same name and the same blood that produced volunteers in the last war should produce volunteers in
the next. If they fail to do so, there is a reason. The result is that a government which knows it is going to be confronted with war should become particularly anxious to see that people can get work, that they are well nourished, that they are given something to cause them to hope. And I may say, with all due respect to the present government, and not wishing to be unkind, that we have not succeeded in producing these conditions in this country. The result is that a good many people who have power are fearful, and with good reason. If they want volunteers to fight their wars let them be warned that they had better produce conditions which bring on volunteers, and not resort to the base and un-British method of conscription.
While I am on this subject, there is another matter to which I shall briefly allude. There is a grave falling off in the birth-rate among all the British peoples. We might be able to go through the next war, but if we continue with the birth-rate we have to-day in comparison with the birth-rates which are becoming common in some of the rival nations, I doubt very much that we shall be able to go successfully through many wars. Something must be done about the matter.
Another consideration is this:	We must
treat our returned men right. I am not going to say anything about this topic. I spoke upon it at some length the other night, with the result that Hansard, at least, knows what I think about our mistreatment of veterans. Certainly we are not treating our returned men as we should, and the reaction upon our youth who see the suffering that has been inflicted upon past heroes is that they are not particularly anxious to be heroes like these veterans. We do a great deal of building up of fine monuments, such as we have in front of this building, but I submit that the finest monument we can raise to the men who fought for their country and passed on is to build up a generation equal to them in strength, prowess, courage, hope and all that goes to make men.
There is another matter which we must look to if we are going to have volunteers. We must take precautions to prevent war profiteering. I wish to commend the government for the actions they have already taken in this regard, but I do not think they have gone nearly far enough. They probably do not, either. There is altogether too much influence of munitions manufacturers in national propaganda. While I am not going to speak to any extent about that, it is not because I am not aware of it. Some pretty nasty rumours have gone round the country during



Foreign Policy-Mr. Blackmore
the last six years. It is not particularly in Canada that I have heard them; nevertheless I imagine that some munition money is being used to influence opinion even in Canada. If we are to create a sound British race, able to meet its foes, we must see to it by every means at our disposal that this sort of thing is eliminated. We must prevent false representations. We must give some sort of guarantee that our people are not going to be utterly crushed by debt. I believe the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) has sufficiently dealt with that point; I shall, therefore, say nothing about it. All these are matters which wise statesmen will be looking to if they are going to depend upon volunteers to fight their wars.
We now come to the fifth question: Can Canada help to remove the causes of war? This is a vital matter. Conceivably we could organize this world in such a way that we could suppress Hitler within three months, simply by removing the causes which have fed his growth. What are those causes? The general causes of war are about five. Men fight for personal ambition, racial ambition, religion, ideologies; but above all they fight for economic necessities; and generally when they fight for any one of the first four causes I have mentioned, the element of economic necessity is not very far distant; it is underneath.
I should like to put on Hansard a few figures to indicate the economic necessity under which Germany and Italy are striving, so that we may realize that, when Hitler tells us he has a case, he may not be telling us what is entirely false. It is so easy, when we become all charged with emotion, as we are- and it is well that we are

to forget to find out the other fellow's point of view. If we are going to remove the curse of war and learn to live at peace in this world, we must find out the other fellow's point of view and adjust ourselves somewhat to it.
Here is a set of figures which I drew from a speech by Mr. F. E. Lathe, of the national research council, Ottawa, delivered on June 27, 1938, before the American Association for the Advancement of Science, in the series on Science and Society. These figures indicate the allocation of the world's forest resources:
Per cent of the world's forest area
U.R.S.R	  21-1
British Empire	 21-0
Brazil	 13-4
United States	 9-1
France and dependencies	 3-9
Argentina	 3-5
Japan	 1-2
Germany and Austria		0-5
Italy and Abyssinia	 0-4
[Mr. Blackmore.)
And we wonder why they fight. May I just recall again the figures which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) quoted not long ago, when he said that three nations, Germany, Italy and Japan, with a total population of about 200,000,000, were trying to keep those people within an area a little bit bigger than Ontario, where we are unable to keep 4,000,000. All we need do is to imagine ourselves in Germany and surmise what we would do if we were in Hitler's place.
I turn to another set of figures which are equally revealing, the coal reserves of the world:
Millions of metric tons
United States	 3.838.657
British Empire	 1,729,105
China	 995,587
Germany and Austria	 477,232
U.S.S.R	   173,879
France and dependencies	 37,585
Japan	 7,970
Italy	 243
Contrast Italy's 243,000,000 tons with our
1,729,105,000.000 tons. There are in this world such things as "have-not" nations. Up to the present time we have not discovered a way whereby Italy, for example, can get the benefit of Alberta's coal fields without possessing Alberta. Until we can learn some way by which we can enable Italy to get such advantages, we must expect war, and if we really wish to remove the causes of war we must set to work to find a way of distributing those goods other than through trade. Many think that trade will do it. Let me tell the house, in all humility, that the more men learn, the more they will realize that trade will not any longer distribute adequately.
There is another set of figures which I was going to put on record, but I shall not take the time. This is a moat remarkable set of figures, which I put on Hansard some time ago, dealing with national sufficiency in major minerals. It shows that whereas the British empire is, as a whole, completely self-sufficient in coal, iron, copper, lead, zinc, and nickel, lacking somewhat in tin and petroleum, Japan is lacking in every one of these, Italy in practically all, and Germany in a good many of them.
May I now turn to the next question. What of collective security? There are a good many people who are much influenced by the idea of collective security. I said last year that I was rather in ined to the idea of collective security if I i <uld find out with whom I was to associate, it is easy enough to talk about collective sec city until you get down to brass tacks, but when you begin to look for the group of nations with whom you are to associate to better advantage than you can

Foreign Policy-Mr. Green
with the members of the British empire you will experience some difficulty in finding those nations.
Just to help us to think our way through, let us suppose a few possible combinations. Suppose we had all the north and south American countries and Belgium, Holland, Denmark and Sweden. Most hon. members would rather favour that group as being congenial society with which to associate. Well, let us ask ourselves three or four questions. In the first place, after you had formed the association, who would decide when you were going to fight, where, and to what extent? In that combination who would make the decision? Would you expect to decide it in this parliament? If you did not, where then would your democracy be? Here we are busily engaged throughout the country sedulously asserting that we are not going to let Britain decide when we shall fight. At the same time some would be ready to grant to a board, consisting of representatives of each of strange nations, the right to decide for us a question concerning which we would not trust Britain. That line of reasoning does not appeal to me. There may be considerations that I have overlooked, but it certainly rouses suspicion in my mind.
Now, suppose <we had agreed who was going to decide whether we were going to fight, and when, where and to what extent. That having been settled, let us ask ourselves this question: Would we commit Canada to an expedition to Holland to protect that country in case of attack? If we say no; if we will not go to protect Holland, then how can we expect Holland to come and protect us if we are in trouble? And if Holland will not protect us and we will not protect Holland, what is the virtue of our collective security? It was a series of questions such as these that brought about the break-down of the League of Nations. It is easy for us to rail against the League of Nations and the people who, we fancy, were responsible for the break-down of the league, but I am inclined to think the rock upon which the League of Nations met shipwreck was composed of just such questions as these. Really no one in particular was responsible; I am inclined to that belief. Consequently, I am a little doubtful about collective security. I wish to get as much as I can out of the idea, but before I trust it too far I should like to have a few of these questions answered.
Suppose, instead of that amiable company which I have indicated, we decided to associate with the United States. Again, let us ask ourselves a few questions. Would you go to defend California in the event of that
state being attacked? If you say no, how can you expect the Californians to come over here to protect Nova Scotians in case they were attacked? And if you go to protect the Californians in case of attack there, what is the difference between that and going to France to protect the French or to Belgium to protect the Belgians? In either instance you are going to fight on foreign soil. I really cannot answer these questions to my own satisfaction. I do not wish it to be supposed that I do not value the League of Nations. The League of Nations is another notable possibility from which we might expect to derive some benefit; but there are fundamental principles that have to be laid down, and once laid down they must be adhered to. If we are not prepared to commit ourselves to a policy of hewing to those lines, then we cannot expect the League of Nations to work. Well, there is the question as to who should determine when, where and to what extent Canadians should fight. Would Canada commit herself, under the League of Nations, to fight at any time in any place and to any extent that a League of Nations committee might decide that she should? I do not think Canada would, because the minute she did she would destroy her democratic rights.
We must be free as a Canadian people to decide for ourselves. Our government must hold itself free to do what the Canadian people from week to week want it to do. This world is changing so fast that we simply cannot say to-day what we shall be thinking and what we shall be ready to do a month from now. In a general way we will lay down the rule that the principles of democracy must be maintained, but that at the same time we are resolved to defend civilization, to defend our liberties, to defend our soil. In the effort to defend these we will not submit to conscription but will rather depend upon the voluntary principle which has seen our fathers through their vicissitudes and which, I think, we can depend upon to take us through our vicissitudes and our children through theirs. That is the nearest we can at present come to determining what for Canada is a sound foreign policy.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thi3 debate has lasted now for three full days, and during the whole of that time the attention of the house has been focused on the European situation. That is only natural, because the tension there has been so much greater during the last few weeks. I would, however, remind hon. members of the inscrip-

Foreign Policy-Mr. Green
tion we see every morning when coming through the main door of the House of Commons:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
I stress that word "both"; for, after all, we have great sea lanes coming to and going from both our Atlantic and Pacific coasts. These sea lanes are ocean highways enabling us to carry our great export business overseas. But also they bring us great problems, which force us to adopt far-reaching and farsighted policies. To-night I propose to deal only with the problems which are brought to the Canadian people by the great Pacific ocean.
On that ocean the Canadian people come in contact with many peoples: First of all, our fellow people of British stock, the Australians and New Zealanders, the British in China, Singapore, Borneo, Fiji and a string of British islands which reach up above the equator into the northern hemisphere to Fanning island which is just south of the Hawaiian islands. For these British peoples of the Pacific we have naturally the greatest of friendship, and with them we have an extensive trade. I would refer hon. members to Canada 1989, the handbook published under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, page 87, where are listed the principal countries to which Canada sells her commodities. We find there that Australia is our third largest customer, and has been for the last three fiscal years down to 1937-38; and that New Zealand in the fiscal year 1937-38 was our sixth largest customer; before that having been in eighth and seventh places respectively.
Also Canada is vitally affected by the defence policies of these other British peoples. For example, we are protected in part by the great British naval base at Singapore. I do not think there is an hon. member here who would contradict that statement. We are also partly protected by the Australian navy, which, incidentally, is far more powerful than our own. And we are vitally interested in the affairs of these other British peoples for another reason. It is only a matter of a few months or possibly a year or two until we shall have an all-British transpacific airway linked up with Trans-Canada Air Lines. I am convinced that planes will leave Vancouver and go by an all-British route right through to Australia, which will bring us that much closer to and give us that much more interest in the affairs of the people of Australia and New Zealand.
A second group of people on the Pacific with whom we come in contact are our

American cousins, our very good neighbours of the United States. We have them in California, Oregon and Washington, three great progressive states; and we have them in the panhandle of Alaska. I wish to stress that to-night, because the panhandle of Alaska lies in front of Canada for several hundred miles. It makes over half of Canada's western boundary, not coastal at ah [DOT] but an inland boundary. Then we have Alaska proper stretching for over one thousand miles to the west of the Yukon, and we have the Aleutian islands stringing out further west and south for hundreds of miles, really forming a northern outpost of the United States of America. Dutch Harbour in those islands is 2.051 miles from San Francisco, almost half way to Japan, Yokohama being only 2,547 miles from Dutch harbour. Incidentally, Dutch harbour is almost on the shortest direct route from San Francisco to Yokohama.
We also have our American cousins in a southern outpost in the Hawaiian islands, a little farther from San Francisco than Dutch Harbour, 2,091 miles out in the Pacific and only 3,394 miles from Yokohama. These two outposts, the Aleutian islands on the north and Hawaii on the south are really the outpost line for the west coast of Canada as well as of the United States.
And then we have the Americans in Panama, 4,000 miles from Vancouver, almost as far as Japan, and the Panama canal. We have an important contact with the United States of America, in the vital importance of that canal to our Pacific trade. Our wheat, lumber, apples, practically all our trade with the United Kingdom, the eastern seaboard of the United States and many other countries goes through that canal.
The third group with whom we come in contact are the Japanese, a proud, aggressive, militaristic, expansionist people, at present waging an undeclared war against the Chinese; found by the League of Nations, with Canada represented at the meeting, an aggressor nation, a member of the Tokyo-Rome-Berlin triangle and allied with the totalitarian nations against the democracies. Yet with that country we also have extensive trade, largely in raw materials. I think in the last fiscal year, 1937-38, Japan was our fourth largest customer. And arising out of our contacts with the Japanese we have a serious immigration, colonization and settlement question on the Pacific coast. Vancouver is 4,260 miles from Japan just about 100 miles less than the distance from Japan to Sydney, Australia.
Those are the three principal groups of peoples with whom Canada is concerned on the Pacific. Of course there are others: the

Foreign Policy-Mr. Green
Chinese; the French and the Dutch in the East Indies; the Russians, and the people of the South American republics. But I refer especially to-night to these three great groups: the British, the Americans and the Japanese.
That being the background, what is the Pacific policy of Canada to-day? Judging from the statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the house during this present session, Canada's policy on the Pacific may be summed up in two words: "no commitments." On March 14 of this year on the orders of the day I called to the attention of the Prime Minister a press dispatch which set forth that there was to be a conference on Pacific defence questions held at Wellington. New Zealand, at which there would be representatives from the United Kingdom. Australia and New Zealand; and I asked:
In view of the fact that Canada has serious defence problems on the Pacific ocean, will it be possible for Canadian representatives to be sent to this conference?
The reply of the Prime Minister was to the effect that Canada had not been invited; that presumably Canada was not concerned and that we would be unwise to accept an invitation until we had it; in other words, that Canada was making no commitments.
With regard to the United States the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) on February 2 of this year referred the Prime Minister to a press dispatch containing some suggestion that Canada and the United States were preparing to defend the continent from invasion on a joint cooperative basis, and the hon. member wanted to know whether or not there was anything in that report. The Prime Minister's answer was as follows, found on page 540 of Hansard:
I gather, however, that the purport of the question is this: Are there any commitments on the part of the present government with the government of the United States in respect of the defence of the Pacific coast. If that is the question I answer that there are no commitments that I am aware of, and I think I should be aware of any if there were.
Mr. .Woodsworth: There was the other prior question which 1 asked as to whether it was correct that there is an arrangement to defend this continent from invasion, involving joint cooperative action, or to what extent the statement is correct.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I should think that an arrangement would be in the nature of a commitment and, I repeat, there is no commitment.
I would point out to the Prime Minister that this means great uncertainty, not only for the Australians, the New Zealanders, the British, the Americans and the Japanese, but
also for our own Canadian people, as to where Canada stands on the Pacific. In my opinion this government always entirely overlooks the effect that a firm stand in foreign affairs would have on our friends, our potential enemies and our own people. Such a wishy-washy policy is neither safe nor sane.
I suggest that the time has come for Canada to adopt as a basic Pacific policy full 

and I repeat that word "full"-and open cooperation with the other British peoples living on the shores of that ocean, and with the American people. I suggest that Canada might enter a defensive alliance with these peoples and I stress the word "defensive." I would point out to the house that neither the British nor the Americans will ever be aggressors on the Pacific, and that our aims and interests are the same. Not only should Canada be sitting in at the defence conference in New Zealand; I suggest that Canada also should have tried to get the United States invited to sit in. As a matter of fact, we already have a defensive alliance with the other countries of the empire. I would refer the house to the summary of proceedings of the last imperial conference, held in 1937. At page 15, dealing with defence, we find this:
The conference gave close attention to the subject of defence, and considered ways in which it would be possible for the governments concerned to cooperate in measures for their own security. The occasion was taken for a detailed review of the state of defence in each of the countries represented at the conference and this opportunity was generally welcomed.
Other statements are found at pages 18 and 19 which make it absolutely clear that as far as Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain are concerned, Canada is or should consider herself to be in a defensive alliance with these countries. I suggest that at the present time Canada should confer with these countries on defence plans, just as she did at the imperial conference. Further, we should provide proper subsidies for the construction of new passenger ships which are so badly needed in order to facilitate trade between our Pacific coast and Australia and New Zealand. I believe we could arrange for the purchase of munitions and armaments from Australia, where they are producing in their state plants more munitions than they need, and consequently are in a position to help supply the needs of the other nations of the empire. And we should ask Great Britain's help in order to establish once more at Esquimalt a north Pacific squadron composed of our own ships and whatever additional ships may be required from the British navy.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Green
Then, Mr. Speaker, instead of relying on a somewhat indefinite, somewhat vague Monroe doctrine or on friendly fleets, which were mentioned last year by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) in presenting his estimates and which obviously meant the United States fleet, since there is no British fleet nearer than Singapore, some seven or eight thousand miles away, I suggest that Canada should confer with the United States on defence plans for the Pacific and should negotiate a defensive alliance under which each nation would do its fair share. For example, the United States badly wants a highway to Alaska for military purposes, in order that she' may defend that territory. If the Canadian defence council consider this highway also necessary for the defence of Canada on the Pacific, then let the government deal directly with the government of the United States. The responsibility for negotiating in regard to such a highway lies right here, with this government; yet at the present time the dominion has left all the negotiations to the province of British Columbia, and has stalled the highway by appointing another commission.
My second basic Pacific policy for Canada is to prevent the problem of the Japanese on the Pacific coast from developing into a situation like that of the Sudetens in Czechoslovakia. Oh, the Prime Minister may smile, but ten, fifteen or twenty-five years from now some prime minister may be shedding tears about this very matter at which the right hon. gentleman smiles to-night. In other words, this is a minority problem, and a serious one. I should think both the Canadian and Japanese governments would be anxious to prevent a minority problem from arising in Canada. The difficulty is largely caused by continued immigration. Year after year the people of British Columbia see Japanese settlers coming in. It is true that only a feiw come in each year, but over the course of a feiw years the number runs into thousands. These people are spreading out into new lines of activity all the time. At page 9 of the report of the government's own board of review, dated October 12 last, I find this:
... all the different types of Japanese activity in the province-agriculture, lumbering, fishing, retail trade and personal service.
They go on to list some of them: farming, lumbering, fish saltery, fishing, shipbuilding, railroading, paper making, fish-canning, berrygrowing, whaling, logging, small fruits, retail trade, rooming houses and so on; they are in many branches of the retail trade; we have

Japanese stores scattered all over the city of Vancouver. And the people of British Columbia firmly believe that their living is being taken away from them and their children by these Japanese immigrants, and that perhaps the coast itself will be taken away from their children eventually.

speechtext:
I have not figures for 1938-39. The last report of the Department of Mines and Resources gives 139 Japanese immigrants during 1937-38, and there have been three or four thousand of them since 1925. Another factor is that nearly all the Japanese stay on the coast. Over ninety per cent of the Japanese in Canada are in British Columbia, whereas only sixty per cent of the Chinese reside in that province. Year after year practically all these immigrants settle in British Columbia. In the last year for which we have a report, 1937-38, every Japanese immigrant is listed as having settled in our province.
And the people of British Columbia know that our province has a far larger percentage of Japanese settlers than any other western country. I should like to quote some statistics prepared by our own bureau, from the census figures of 1931. In that year British Columbia had a total population of 694,263, with a Chinese population of 27,139 and a Japanese population of 22,205. The state of Washington, our neighbour to the south, with twice our population, had one-twelfth the number of Chinese and three-quarters the number of Japanese. Oregon, still further to the south, with one and a half times our population, had one-thirteenth the number of Chinese and one-quarter the number of Japanese. California, with eight times our population, had one and a half times the number of Chinese and four times the number of Japanese. In other words, in proportion we had twice as many Japanese as the state of California. In Australia, where there was a population of
6.600.000	in 1933, there were about 11,000 Chinese and only 2,241 Japanese, as against 22,205 Japanese in British Columbia. In all these other states and in Australia immigration was stopped years ago. In Canada Chinese immigration was stopped in 1923, but Japanese immigration still goes on. It is estimated by the provincial government that there are now not 22,000 but actually between 25,000 and
30.000	Japanese in our province.
Then, we must remember that more than half the immigrants are women. In the last year, out of 139 immigrants ninety-six were

Foreign Policy-Mr. Green
women and only forty-three men. Practically all the women were of marriageable age. I should like to quote to the house from a brief prepared by the junior board of trade of Vancouver and submitted to the national convention of the junior chamber of commerce of Canada which was held in Montreal last October. This brief shows the births per thousand from the vital statistics of the Vancouver health department and the natural increase per thousand of population:
Births per Natural increase thousand per thousand Per cent	Per cent
General	 11-18
Japanese	 28-8
Chinese	 8-11
20-8
(5-92)decrease
The brief goes on to state:
These are Vancouver figures only. For British Columbia the Japanese natural increase per thousand is twenty-five and for whites it is five. The Japanese birth-rate in British Columbia is forty per 1,000 compared with fifteen for other races.
I would point out that the people of British Columbia will never give in on this question. They grow more determined every year that further immigration must be stopped. Not only would it benefit us, but it would benefit the Japanese already in the province, because every new immigrant makes the position of the Japanese already there just that much more difficult. It means more competition, and far less chance of there being a better feeling between the races.
This matter has been dealt with recently by political parties in Canada. In convention last summer the National Conservative party passed this resolution:
That the Canadian government should take effective measures for the exclusion of orientals from Canada by strict enforcement of the existing statutes and regulations and by taking the necessary steps to secure the rescission of the Lemieux agreement.
Which is the agreement under which the Japanese enter Canada. That resolution was endorsed by the convention of the British Columbia Conservative Association. A similar resolution was adopted by the Liberal Association in British Columbia, and the Liberal government of that province passed this resolution at the session held last fall.
Whereas British Columbia is one of the most important provinces of the Dominion of Canada

I would say the most important.
-and whereas it is necessary for the social and economic welfare of our people that our population sha'l be ethnologieally homogeneous:-	[DOT]
Those are Liberal words-
-therefore be it resolved, that this house goes on record as being opposed to the immigration
of any Japanese or Chinese into the province of British Columbia, and commends the action of the provincial government in making representations to the Ottawa government to this end.
The Liberal government in Ottawa last year refused to adopt a measure to stop further immigration. I think the junior board of trade of Vancouver summed up the situation very well in their brief when they recorded these two lines:
When times are good the Japanese question must not be mentioned because we might lose Japanese trade. When times are bad, well, Japan might attack us.
Those are the excuses put forward by the federal government. I suggest that at this time the Canadian government should ask the Japanese government to agree to stop further immigration. If they cannot do this; if they cannot accomplish the results in that way, then I suggest that the Canadian government should stop it themselves. I suggest further that under section 38 of the Immigration Act they have that power. May I read to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that portion of the section in question which applies:
The governor in council may, by proclamation or order whenever it deems it necessary or expedient. . . .
(c) prohibit or limit in number for a stated period or permanently the landing in Canada, or the landing at any specified port or ports of entry in Canada, of immigrants belonging to any nationality or race or of immigrants of any specified class or occupation, by reason of any economic, industrial or other condition temporarily existing in Canada or because such immigrants are deemed unsuitable having regard to the climatic, industrial, social, educational, labour or other conditions or requirements of Canada or because such immigrants are deemed undesirable owing to their peculiar customs, habits, modes of life and methods of holding property, and because of their probable inability to become readily assimilated-
Which is the difficulty in this case.
-or to assume the duties and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship within a reasonable time after their entry.
Those are the two main policies, which I suggest to the government should be Canada's policies on the Pacific at the present time.
In conclusion I take it from the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that this government's policy of "no commitments" has been thrown overboard-at least so far as European affairs are concerned. I trust it will also go overboard, in so far as affairs on the Pacific are concerned.
For three years we have heard this government prattle about Canada having no commitments. That policy was and is a delusion

Foreign Policy-Mr. Green
and a snare, and I am glad if it is gone. I am glad that Canada, the senior dominion, is no longer hanging back. Now Canadians can once more hold up their heads and look the peoples of other nations in the eye. This new policy is far more nearly in line with the courage, the initiative, and the common sense and friendliness withal of the individual Canadian.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
